Nadia counted the apartments on six floors: 6 × 8 = 48 doors. Two entrances served equal sections, so 48 ÷ 2 = 24 apartments per entrance. She then added the listed processing periods: 15 + 20 + 35 = 70 minutes. Since 25 minutes had passed after the last scan, 70 - 25 = 45 minutes were unaccounted for. At 9:00, she checked again. The shelf still held 9 parcels, and a courier added 4 more, making 9 + 4 = 13. None displayed her apartment number, so Nadia returned upstairs.

Rain tapped the apartment windows as Javier checked the empty hallway outside his door. The tracking page claimed his package had been delivered at 3:17, yet the photograph showed only a black square. Inside it were copies of documents, a spare key, and a flash drive containing evidence against his former employer. He called the courier, but the operator said someone had signed for it. “Who signed?” Javier asked. The operator read his own name. A floorboard creaked above him, though the upstairs apartment had stood vacant for weeks. His phone buzzed with a message from an unknown number: We opened it. Javier’s throat tightened. He locked the deadbolt, then dragged a chair beneath the handle. Another message appeared, displaying a photograph of him staring at the screen, taken through the rain-streaked window. His pulse hammered against his ribs. The hallway light went out. Slow footsteps stopped outside his door, and a key slid into the lock.

Javier checked the space beside the front door before leaving for work. The package was not there. He opened the delivery page on his phone and read the latest entry, which said the parcel remained in transit. At the bus stop, he put the phone in his pocket and watched two buses pass before his route arrived. During lunch, he checked the page again. The entry had not changed. After work, Javier walked home by the usual streets and stopped at the building’s mailboxes. He sorted through an envelope, a grocery flyer, and a utility notice. The package was not among them. Upstairs, he asked a neighbor, “Did a parcel come for me?” The neighbor said, “Not today.” Javier entered his apartment, placed the mail on the counter, and looked near the balcony door. He then made rice and vegetables, washed the pan, and checked the delivery page once more. The same entry remained. Before bed, he left the hallway light on for a minute, checked outside, and closed the door.

Rain traced the apartment windows as Javier sat beside the unopened mail slot. For six days, the tracking page had displayed the same line: delayed in transit. The package held the final recordings his father had made before dying, cassette tapes mailed by a nurse after the funeral. Javier refreshed the page until the letters blurred. At noon, the courier called and explained that the parcel had been damaged at a sorting depot; its contents could not be recovered. “I’m sorry,” the voice said. Javier lowered the phone without answering. He pictured brown tape peeling away, black cassettes crushed beneath machinery, his father’s voice spilling into a place where nobody knew him. His chest tightened. He slid to the floor and pressed his forehead against his knees. The mail slot clicked, dropping a grocery coupon behind him, but he did not turn. By evening, the tracking page still promised delivery, and Javier kept staring at it while tears darkened his sleeves.

Rain streaked the apartment windows while delivery trucks crawled along the avenue below. Javier refreshed the tracking page again: PACKAGE DELIVERED, 2:14 P.M. The lobby shelf stood empty, and the building camera showed the courier returning to the van with his box tucked under one arm. When Javier called the company, a representative repeated that the scan proved delivery and refused to review the footage. “File a claim in thirty days,” the representative said. Thirty days. The medicine inside was needed tomorrow, and he had paid extra for guaranteed arrival. Heat surged up Javier’s neck. He gripped the phone until his knuckles blanched, listening to the same scripted refusal circle back on itself. His jaw ached from clenching it. They had taken his money, kept his package, and now demanded that he wait as if he were the one making trouble. He slammed the tracking receipt onto the desk, scattering pens, then opened the complaint form and began typing with rigid, punishing strokes.

At nine, Nadia stood beside a red lacquered door and checked the empty brick-colored porch for the package. The courier site displayed a crimson banner above a map, but the parcel marker remained at a vermilion depot. She set her red phone on a scarlet placemat and opened the tracking page again. Outside, a delivery van passed the burgundy mailbox and continued beneath rows of russet leaves. Nadia placed a ruby-colored mug beside a stack of red folders while the clock advanced to ten. At noon, a neighbor crossed the hall carrying a maroon umbrella and said, “No package downstairs.” Nadia recorded the time with a carmine pencil on a sheet edged in red. Later, muted red sunlight spread through the cherry-colored curtains and covered the floorboards. The tracking page changed from crimson to dark garnet, listing a routing delay without a new date. By evening, Nadia closed the red blinds, moved the scarlet placemat, and left the brick-colored porch empty.

Javier waited beside a red door while late afternoon light crossed the crimson tiles. The package tracker displayed a small red map, though the parcel remained listed at a distant depot. He checked the scarlet mailbox, opening its red metal lid and finding only a burgundy catalog. Across the street, a courier arranged maroon crates inside a red van but carried nothing toward his building. Javier returned indoors and placed the catalog on a cherry-colored table beside a ruby glass. A red clock marked five while vermilion shadows shifted along the wall. He called the depot using a phone in a dark red case. “The package has not arrived,” he said. An employee stated that the label had been scanned under a red warehouse lamp and that delivery would be attempted the next day. Javier recorded the update in a notebook with a crimson cover. At dusk, he closed the red curtains, left the empty ruby glass on the table, and set the scarlet mailbox key beside it.

Rain streaked the apartment windows while delivery trucks hissed along the avenue below. Javier refreshed the tracking page again: “Delayed. Location unknown.” The package held a handmade guitar pickup he needed for his first paid performance, now only two days away. He checked the lobby, questioned the doorman, and searched behind every planter, but the shelf remained bare. That evening, while rehearsing with his old, crackling equipment, he heard a knock. A neighbor stood outside holding a battered box that had been left on the wrong floor. Javier recognized the shipping label. His breath caught, and he tore the cardboard open with trembling fingers. Inside, wrapped safely in paper, lay the pickup. He installed it at once, connected his guitar, and struck a chord. The note rang warm and clear through the room. Javier laughed until his ribs hurt, spun once across the rug, and played the chord again. The performance suddenly seemed not merely possible, but destined to soar.

Nadia checked the apartment lobby after breakfast and found the parcel shelf empty. The package had been scheduled for delivery the previous afternoon, but the tracking page still listed it at a regional depot. She returned upstairs, rinsed her cup, and placed it beside the sink. Before starting work, she opened the confirmation email and compared the address with the label information on the order page. The details matched. At noon, a delivery van stopped outside, and Nadia watched from the window as the driver carried several boxes into the neighboring building. She went down again when she took out the recycling, but the shelf remained empty. “Any deliveries?” she asked. The desk attendant replied, “Not since morning.” Nadia collected her mail, returned to her apartment, and set the envelopes on the table. By evening, the tracking page had not changed. She closed the browser, prepared a sandwich, and placed the order receipt in a drawer.

Javier rented a narrow room above the harbor, where seawater tapped the pilings beneath his window. A package had been scheduled for Tuesday, but the coastal courier brought only envelopes marked with salt. On Wednesday, Javier checked the tracking page while fishing boats crossed the bay and gulls circled over the tide line. The listing said the parcel had reached a warehouse beside the northern docks, where ferries moved between low islands. He walked along the seawall to the local depot, passing tide pools occupied by anemones, mussels, and small crabs. “It has not arrived here,” the clerk said as a cargo ship sounded its horn beyond the breakwater. Javier returned by the marina, where ropes rubbed against masts and silver fish turned below the surface. On Thursday, the tracking entry remained unchanged, though the tide covered yesterday’s strips of exposed sand. He placed the delivery notice beside a shell on the windowsill and watched a pilot boat guide another vessel toward the harbor mouth.

At the school science fair, Mateo arranged a red poster board behind three crimson paper cups and a scarlet measuring strip. On the red-covered table, he placed a model watershed molded from rust-red clay and edged with burgundy gravel. A ruby lamp cast red light across the channels, while tinted water moved from a maroon bottle into a clear basin. Mateo recorded each flow time with a red pencil on rose-colored graph paper. Around him, students carried vermilion folders, teachers wore red badges, and visitors followed a brick-red path marked on the floor. When a judge stopped, Mateo pointed to the carmine labels that identified slope, surface texture, and runoff volume. The judge wrote notes on a red clipboard and asked how the measurements had been repeated. Mateo answered that each trial used the same crimson cup, the same amount of tinted water, and the same clay angle. Later, he adjusted a red binder clip, replaced a coral data card, and stood beside the display until the fair ended.

Rain tapped the kitchen window while Nadia refreshed the delivery page beside a mug. The package had not arrived, though the tracker insisted it had been left at her door. Inside was the handmade music box she had saved for all year, intended for her mother’s birthday that evening. She searched the porch, bins, and hedge, then paced from room to room as the rain thickened. A knock finally sounded. On the step stood a soaked neighbor holding a dry cardboard box; the courier had tucked it beneath the wrong awning. Nadia tore open the tape and turned the brass key. The mechanism played perfectly. Her breath caught, then laughter burst from her so hard that she had to brace herself against the doorframe. She hugged the box to her chest, spun once across the hallway, and kissed the neighbor’s wet sleeve. “It works,” she said, barely containing another laugh. When her mother arrived, Nadia wound the key again, her whole face brightening as the melody filled the house.

Nora checked the front step after breakfast, but the package was not there. She looked in the mailbox and found two envelopes and a grocery flyer. Inside, she opened the delivery page on her laptop. The status still said that the parcel was in transit. She copied the tracking code into a note, closed the page, and placed the envelopes beside the fruit bowl. Around midday, a van stopped near the building. A driver carried a box to another entrance, returned to the van, and left. Nora washed a cup, wiped the counter, and checked the step again before taking out the recycling. In the hallway, a neighbor passed with a paper bag. “No delivery today,” the neighbor said. Nora nodded and continued downstairs. Later, she read the shipping notice once more. It gave no new date. She put her laptop away, drew the curtains, and left the empty space by the door unchanged.

Rain traced the apartment windows while delivery trucks moved along the street below. Nora refreshed the tracking page again, watching the same message appear: delayed in transit. The package held the quilt her mother had finished during her final weeks, stitching scraps from childhood dresses into a last gift. For three days, Nora slept beside her phone and hurried downstairs whenever the building door opened. On the fourth morning, a courier called. The truck carrying her parcel had caught fire on the highway; nothing in the cargo compartment had survived. “I’m sorry,” he said. Nora thanked him automatically and set the phone on the table. She opened the closet where one faded dress still hung, its hem missing the square her mother had cut away. Pressing the empty gap between her fingers, Nora sank to the floor. Her breath came in shallow pulls. She pictured the quilt’s bright pieces curling into black ash, and understood that no one could remake what those hands had made.

Rain ticked against the lobby windows as Nora stood beside the empty parcel shelf. The tracking page claimed her package had been delivered at noon, signed for with a crooked version of her name. She showed the screen to the building manager, who barely glanced at it before shrugging. “Nothing I can do.” Behind his desk, Nora spotted the retailer’s bright tape on a crushed box, its label turned downward. When she pointed, he pulled it beneath the counter and said it belonged to someone else. Heat surged up her neck. She had waited three weeks, paid extra for secure delivery, and now he was hiding it while dismissing her. Her jaw locked. She slapped her receipt onto the desk, rattling the pen cup, then reached over and spun the box around. Her name filled the label. “Open the cabinet.” The manager went pale. Nora planted both palms on the counter, pulse hammering, and refused to move until he surrendered her package.

Rain streaked the apartment windows as Nora checked the lobby mailboxes after dusk. The package containing her replacement house keys was two days late, though the courier’s website insisted it had been delivered. She searched behind planters, beneath the stairs, and beside the trash bins. Nothing. Returning upstairs, she noticed a torn strip of cardboard wedged under her door. Her address was printed on it. Inside, muddy footprints crossed the entryway and stopped beside her bedroom. Nora’s breath snagged. She backed into the hall, fumbling for her phone, but the screen showed no signal. From the bedroom came the slow scrape of a drawer opening. Her pulse hammered against her throat. She remembered the spare key included in the missing parcel and pictured someone watching the courier leave. The bedroom floor creaked. A shadow stretched across the wall toward her. Nora ran for the stairwell, bare feet slipping on the tiles, while behind her the apartment door swung wider with a soft click.

Rain striped the apartment windows while delivery vans moved through the street below. Oskar refreshed the tracking page again, but the package still showed as delayed, four days after its promised arrival. Inside it was a repaired music box that had belonged to his grandfather, returned from a workshop across the country. He checked the lobby, called the depot, and searched behind the bins. Nothing. Near dusk, footsteps sounded on the stairs, followed by a knock. A soaked courier stood outside holding a dented brown parcel. “This was left in the wrong building.” Oskar’s hands shook as he signed. He tore the tape, lifted away the paper, and turned the tiny brass key. The old melody spilled into the room, clear and bright. His breath burst out as laughter. He spun once across the kitchen, then cradled the box against his chest, grinning until his cheeks hurt. Every note seemed impossible and perfect, and he played it again.

Nora checked the lobby shelf at 8:10, but the package had not arrived. The tracking page listed four transit stops across 360 kilometers, so she calculated 360 ÷ 4 = 90 kilometers per segment. It had left the depot at 6:25; adding 3 hours and 45 minutes gave 10:10. She compared that estimate with the clock, which read 9:20, and found 10:10 − 9:20 = 50 minutes remaining. The parcel contained 6 boxes of filters, with 8 filters in each box, so 6 × 8 = 48 filters. Her cabinet still held 17; adding the shipment would produce 17 + 48 = 65. At 10:15, the shelf remained empty. A clerk said, “The afternoon truck carries delayed parcels.” Nora recorded that update. The truck’s route included 12 buildings and allowed 5 minutes per building, making 12 × 5 = 60 minutes. If it started at 1:30, then 1:30 + 60 minutes = 2:30. She returned upstairs and continued cataloging the 17 filters already present.

Javier checked the apartment lobby at 9:10, but the package had not arrived. He opened the carrier’s tracking page and copied six time stamps into a notebook. The route listed 18 stops; the driver had completed 11, so 18 minus 11 equaled 7 remaining. Javier estimated four minutes per stop: 7 times 4 equaled 28 minutes. Adding 28 minutes to 9:10 produced 9:38. At 9:42, the lobby shelf still held only three envelopes and two boxes, for 3 plus 2 equals 5 items. He measured the empty space: 60 centimeters divided by 4 equal sections gave 15 centimeters per section. The manifest showed a 24-by-16-centimeter carton, so it would occupy two sections if placed sideways. Javier returned upstairs and compared earlier transit intervals: 36 minutes plus 44 minutes equaled 80; 80 divided by 2 equaled a 40-minute average. At 10:05, he checked again. The shelf count remained five, the tracking status remained “out for delivery,” and Javier recorded the new time.

Rain streaked the kitchen window while Nora refreshed the tracking page on her phone. The package had been marked “out for delivery” three days earlier, yet the porch remained bare. Inside it was the handmade quilt she had spent six months sewing for her sister’s new baby, returned by the hospital gift service after an address error. She checked the hedge, the bins, and even the empty shed, then called the courier again. As she waited, a van slowed at the gate. The driver climbed out holding a battered brown box, its label smeared but legible. Nora signed so quickly that the pen skidded across the screen. She carried the parcel inside, peeled back the damp cardboard, and found the quilt dry, bright, and perfectly folded beneath its ribbon. Her breath burst into a laugh. She pressed the soft stars to her face, spun once across the tiles, and read the corrected hospital address three times. “You’re going to make it,” she whispered, already reaching for fresh wrapping.

Rain traced the kitchen window while Oskar sat beside the telephone and watched the empty road. The package had been due three days earlier, and each van that passed made him rise from his chair. Inside it was the final recording his brother had made from the hospital, along with the watch their father had given him. Oskar had declined a digital copy; he wanted to hear the tape turning in the old player they had shared as boys. At noon, the courier called. “The parcel was destroyed in a depot fire.” Oskar asked whether anything had survived, but the answer dissolved beneath the blood beating in his ears. He lowered the telephone and remained standing, one hand gripping the table. The missed hospital calls returned to him, then his brother’s last message: wait for the package. Oskar opened the front door anyway. Rain blew across the threshold. He sank onto the step, pressed both fists against his mouth, and rocked until night erased the road.

Rain striped the windows of Oskar’s apartment while delivery vans crawled along the street below. His tracking page claimed his package had been delivered at noon, yet the lobby, stairs, and mailroom were bare. He checked the photograph attached as proof. It showed a brown box outside a different building, its number clearly visible. When he called the courier, a clerk repeated that the scan was final and refused to open a case. “The system says you received it.” Oskar stared at the photograph until heat climbed his neck. He had paid extra for secure delivery, waited ten days, and now a stranger hid behind a system that contradicted its own evidence. His grip tightened around the phone. He demanded a supervisor, but the line went dead. Oskar slammed the phone onto the table, rattling every cup. Then he printed the photograph, circled the wrong number in red until the paper tore, and marched downstairs to wait beside the entrance for the next courier van.

Nora lived above a harbor where gulls crossed the windows and fishing boats shifted with the tide. A package she had ordered was due on Monday, but the coastal courier van passed her building without stopping. She checked the tracking page while seawater tapped the pilings beneath her room. The status said the parcel had reached a depot beyond the headland, near a beach marked by rows of pale shells. On Tuesday, Nora walked along the quay, where nets dried beside moored trawlers and small crabs moved between stones. A clerk at the harbor counter scanned the number and said, “It is still in transit.” Nora returned home as ferries traced white lines across the bay. Wednesday brought a low tide, several seals on a sandbar, and no package. By Thursday, the tracking page listed another coastal depot farther north, where cargo ships waited beyond the breakwater. Nora placed the delivery note beside a bowl of sea glass and watched the evening tide cover the mudflats.

Oskar checked the entryway at 9:10, but the package had not arrived. The tracking page listed 12 stops before his building. At 9:40, 5 stops remained, so he calculated that the driver had completed 12 - 5 = 7 stops in 30 minutes. That rate was 7 ÷ 30 = 0.233 stops per minute. He measured the empty shelf reserved for the parcel: 40 centimeters by 25 centimeters, giving 40 × 25 = 1,000 square centimeters of surface. The package dimensions were listed as 32 by 18 centimeters, leaving 40 - 32 = 8 centimeters lengthwise and 25 - 18 = 7 centimeters across. At 10:20, the page showed 3 stops. Two more had been completed in 40 minutes, or 40 ÷ 2 = 20 minutes per stop. Oskar added the intervals: 30 + 40 = 70 minutes. He checked again at 10:50. The package still had not arrived, so he closed the page and used the shelf for four folders.

Oskar lived above a harbor where seawater tapped the pilings beneath his window. Each morning, he checked the entryway for a package while fishing boats crossed the silver tide. The parcel contained brass hinges for a cabinet in his coastal workshop, but the delivery notice still listed it aboard a ferry. At noon, gulls circled the docks as Oskar examined the empty shelf beside the marine charts. A courier arrived along the quay, carrying three boxes marked with shipping routes and whale symbols. “Nothing for this address,” the courier said while a seal surfaced near the seawall. Oskar recorded the date in a ledger decorated with blue waves. He then sanded driftwood as cargo vessels moved beyond the breakwater. By evening, the tide had lowered around the moored sailboats, and no parcel stood by his door. Oskar closed the workshop, placed the unfinished cabinet beside a jar of shells, and watched the ferry lights proceed along the coastline.

Beatriz arrived at the municipal pitch carrying her boots and a bottle of water. She changed beside the low wooden bench, tied her laces, and joined the other players for a brief warm-up. The referee checked both goals while several spectators stood along the fence. When the match began, Beatriz played on the right side of midfield. She received a pass, moved the ball forward, and sent it toward a teammate near the penalty area. A defender cleared it over the touchline. “Your throw,” the referee said. Beatriz collected the ball and passed it back into play. During the second half, she tracked an opposing player, blocked a cross, and later took a corner that landed near the goalkeeper. The final whistle came after an equal score. Players shook hands, gathered jackets and bags, and left the field. Beatriz wiped mud from her boots with a cloth, drank some water, and walked toward the bus stop.

On Saturday afternoon, Beatriz stood at left wing on a muddy municipal pitch while neighbors lined the touchline. Her amateur team trailed by one goal with three minutes remaining, and her socks clung heavily to her shins. When a defender slipped, Beatriz collected the loose ball and sprinted forward, hearing teammates pound the ground behind her. She crossed low; a striker met it, and the ball rattled into the net. “One more,” Beatriz called, racing back. In the final minute, a corner dropped through a tangle of legs and bounced toward her. She swung without thinking. The shot skimmed the grass, struck the inside post, and rolled over the line. For a heartbeat she stared. Then she leaped so high her knees tucked beneath her, and a shout burst from her chest. Teammates surrounded her, thumping her back and lifting her off the mud. Her face ached from grinning. As the whistle sounded, she thought the whole gray afternoon had turned golden.

On Sunday afternoon, two amateur teams gathered on a muddy municipal pitch beneath sagging floodlights. Beatriz played forward, chasing long passes while spectators stamped beside the touchline. Late in the second half, she slipped between two defenders and struck the ball into the net. The referee pointed toward the center, then reversed his decision after the opposing captain protested. He claimed Beatriz had handled the ball, though her arms had been pinned against her ribs. “That never touched my hand,” she said. The referee waved her away and booked her. Heat surged up her neck. Her jaw locked, and she dug her studs into the turf, imagining the whistle crushed beneath her boot. Minutes later, a defender shoved her down inside the penalty area. Play continued. Beatriz sprang up, mud streaking her knees, and sprinted after the referee, fists clenched so hard her nails cut her palms. At the final whistle, she kicked the corner flag flat and stalked away without shaking anyone’s hand.

At noon, Nora stood beside the red mailbox and checked the tracking page for a package scheduled that morning. It still showed the parcel at a depot across town, marked by a crimson square. She set her red phone on a brick-colored shelf and sorted the mail: a scarlet brochure, a rust-red envelope, and a catalog with a cherry border. Outside, a courier in a maroon cap pushed a burgundy cart past the vermilion gate without stopping. Nora opened the red curtains, and ruby light from a tinted window crossed the floor. “No delivery yet,” she said to the tenant watering geraniums in a red pot. The tenant noted that several parcels remained at the crimson-painted depot. Nora returned to her desk, placed a red pencil beside the receipt, and entered the new tracking time. By dusk, the package had not arrived, while red lamplight lay across its empty place on the mat. She closed the russet curtains and left the red mailbox unchecked until morning.

The amateur teams gathered on a muddy pitch behind the village hall as evening clouds covered the floodlights. Beatriz played at right back, slipping often but clearing every ball that reached her. Late in the second half, a clearance sailed over the fence and struck a parked van. Its alarm began shrieking. A large man climbed out, pulled a metal bar from behind his seat, and strode toward the pitch. “Who did that?” he called. The players scattered toward the changing rooms, but Beatriz stood nearest the ball. The man fixed his eyes on her and raised the bar. Her throat closed. Cold prickles raced across her scalp, and her knees shook so violently that her studs clicked together. She pictured the bar crashing into her skull and could not draw a full breath. When he stepped over the low fence, she finally ran. Mud dragged at her boots. She reached the hall, slammed the door, and crouched behind it while his footsteps approached.

On Sunday afternoon, two amateur football teams gathered on a muddy municipal pitch beneath low clouds. Beatriz tied her boots beside the touchline while her father watched from his usual folding chair, wrapped in a red scarf. He had attended every match since teaching her to kick a ball between flowerpots. Late in the second half, with the score level, Beatriz met a cross and headed it into the net. She turned toward him, raising both arms, but the chair stood empty. Beyond the barrier, several spectators crowded around a figure on the ground. The referee stopped play. Beatriz ran over and recognized the red scarf beneath a stranger’s hands. “Please, let me through,” she said. An ambulance came, then departed without its siren. The match was abandoned. Beatriz remained on the pitch after everyone left, gripping the soaked scarf against her mouth. Her winning goal meant nothing now. She sank beside the vacant chair, shoulders convulsing, and stared at the flowerpot mud caked on her boots.

Oskar stood beside the red gate at noon, holding a crimson delivery card under the red porch lamp. A scarlet van passed the house but continued beyond the row of red brick walls. He checked the tracking page on his phone, whose ruby case matched the dark-red mailbox. The page listed the parcel as delayed, with no new time beneath the vermilion header. Oskar opened the mailbox and found a red grocery leaflet, two rust-colored envelopes, and no package. Across the pavement, a courier arranged maroon cartons beneath a burgundy awning. “Nothing for this address,” the courier said, setting a small red box onto a trolley. Oskar returned indoors, where red curtains filtered the afternoon into muted carmine bands. He placed the crimson card beside a red ceramic bowl and refreshed the tracking page once. The status remained unchanged, while a red clock marked another minute and the unopened space on the table stayed empty.

Rain ticked against the windows of Oskar’s apartment as evening traffic crawled below. The medical courier’s package had been due at noon, and the tracking page still showed it crossing town. Inside were the replacement cartridges that kept his implanted pump working. At eight, the pump chirped once. Oskar checked its display: RESERVOIR LOW. He called the courier, but a recorded voice said the office was closed. Then the tracking page refreshed. DELIVERED, it read, signed for by Oskar. His mouth went dry. He tore open his door and searched the corridor, stairs, and lobby, finding only wet footprints that ended beside the basement door. The pump chirped again, longer this time. His hands shook so badly that he dropped his phone. Someone had taken the parcel, and whoever signed his name knew what it contained. A scrape sounded below. Oskar backed into the wall, clutching the pump through his shirt, while the basement handle slowly began to turn.

Beatriz arrived at the amateur football pitch at 14:10, twenty minutes before kickoff at 14:30. She counted 12 players, then two more arrived, so 12 + 2 = 14. The group divided into two teams: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 players per side. Beatriz marked the field with eight cones along each touchline, using 8 × 2 = 16 cones in total. During the first half, her team attempted nine passes through midfield; six reached their targets, leaving 9 − 6 = 3 incomplete passes. At halftime, the score was 1–1. The organizer set 15 minutes for the second half, and Beatriz calculated that two equal periods made 15 × 2 = 30 minutes of play. Her side took four shots after the interval, while the other side took three, giving 4 + 3 = 7 shots. One shot entered each goal, and the match ended 2–2. Beatriz collected 16 cones, divided them into four stacks of 16 ÷ 4 = 4, and left at 15:12.

Rain streaked the floodlights above the muddy municipal football pitch as two amateur teams lined up for the final minutes. Bruno’s side trailed by one goal, and his shirt clung to his back while spectators stamped along the touchline. A loose pass skidded toward him near midfield. He trapped it, slipped between two defenders, and drove forward, hearing teammates call behind him. The goalkeeper rushed out. Bruno nudged the ball aside and was clipped, but he stayed upright and rolled a shot toward the far post. It struck the upright, spun across the line, and settled in the net. The referee’s whistle ended the match before the restart. Bruno froze, staring at the ball, then flung both arms skyward. Laughter burst from him in breathless waves. His teammates piled around him, thumping his shoulders and smearing mud across his face. “We did it,” he gasped. His chest seemed too small for the warmth surging through it, and he wanted that soaked, shining moment to last forever.

Beatriz arrived at the harbor pitch while the tide slid between the pilings. Beyond one touchline, fishing boats shifted on seawater, and gulls crossed the pale coastline. She joined the amateur team beside a net that carried dried strands of seaweed. The referee placed the ball at midfield as small waves tapped the stone quay. Beatriz played on the left wing, where salt spray marked the grass and shells lined the boundary. During the first half, she passed toward a teammate while a ferry moved across the bay. “Wide again,” the captain said, with the words carrying over the water. Beatriz received the return pass near the corner, as silver fish turned beneath the harbor surface. Her cross reached the penalty area, but a defender sent the ball toward the seawall. After halftime, the teams exchanged possession while the ebb tide exposed dark rocks along the coast. The match ended level, and Beatriz collected two cones as boats followed the channel toward the open sea.

Oskar checked the tracking page after breakfast. The package was still listed at a regional depot, with no delivery time shown. He closed the page, rinsed his cup, and put it on the drying rack. Before leaving for work, he looked through the glass panel beside the building entrance. The floor near the mailboxes was empty. In the afternoon, Oskar returned and found two envelopes in his box, both addressed to other apartments. He placed them in the correct boxes and went upstairs. The tracking page displayed the same depot entry. He prepared potatoes and cabbage, ate at the kitchen table, and wiped the counter. Later, footsteps passed in the corridor and a door opened, but no one knocked. Oskar checked the entrance once more while taking a bag to the bins. No parcel had been left there. He returned to his apartment, set his phone beside the lamp, and noted that the delivery status had not changed.

Beatriz arrived at the amateur football ground wearing a red jersey, maroon shorts, and crimson socks. Red gravel bordered the pitch, while faded scarlet flags marked each corner beneath a copper-red evening sky. The referee carried a burgundy notebook and checked both teams beside a row of red plastic chairs. Beatriz took her position near the center circle, where rust-colored soil showed through the grass. A player in a vermilion bib passed the red-and-white ball toward her, and she redirected it along the left side. “Hold the line,” someone said from beside a crimson equipment bag. Beatriz followed the ball past a brick-red clubhouse, then sent a low pass between two players wearing cherry-colored armbands. Later, the goalkeeper placed the ball beside a dark-red towel and kicked it toward midfield. The match ended level as red light stretched across the pitch. Beatriz collected two scarlet cones, folded a wine-colored training vest, and left through the red gate.

Floodlights shone across the muddy municipal pitch as two amateur teams lined up for the evening match. Bruno wore the captain’s armband and his late father’s faded boots, which had carried him through every season since the funeral. With minutes remaining, the score was level, and a teammate slipped the ball into his path. Bruno struck cleanly, but the shot clipped the post and rolled wide. On the counterattack, their opponents scored. The referee blew for full time before the restart. “Unlucky,” someone said, touching his shoulder. Bruno did not answer. He remained beside the goal while players shook hands and gathered their bags. One boot had split along the sole, exposing the worn leather inside. He crouched and pressed it together, though mud kept seeping through the crack. His chest tightened as he remembered his father polishing those boots at the kitchen table, promising to watch him win in them one day. Bruno lowered his head, and tears dropped onto the ruined leather.

Bruno arrived at the municipal pitch carrying his boots in a cloth bag. He changed beside the fence, tied the laces, and joined the other players for a brief warm-up. One player placed markers along the touchline while another checked the nets. The referee called both teams together, reviewed the basic rules, and started the match. Bruno played on the right side of midfield. He received several passes, returned the ball to nearby teammates, and followed his marker when possession changed. The ground was dry, though a few worn patches made the ball bounce unevenly. During a break in play, Bruno adjusted one sock and drank from a bottle near the bench. The match resumed with a throw-in. Later, he took a corner that was cleared toward the halfway line. The referee ended the game after the usual period. Bruno shook hands with the opposing players, removed his boots, packed his bag, and walked to the bus stop.

Bruno arrived at the harbor pitch while the morning tide slid between rows of moored fishing boats. Saltwater marked the stone wall behind one goal, and gulls crossed above the touchline. He joined the other amateur players, tightened his boots, and watched small waves fold against the quay. The referee placed the ball at midfield as a ferry moved beyond the breakwater. Bruno played on the right wing, where seaweed lay beyond the boundary fence and crabs moved among wet rocks below. He received a pass, carried the ball toward the coastline end, and sent a low cross through the penalty area. A defender cleared it while a trawler sounded its horn offshore. At halftime, the players drank water beside nets hung to dry near the marina. “Same positions,” the captain said as the tide turned. Bruno resumed his runs while sunlight shifted across the bay and silver fish surfaced near the pilings. The match ended level, and he collected the ball as boats returned through the harbor mouth.

Floodlights washed the muddy municipal pitch as two amateur teams gathered for the Saturday match. Bruno started at centre-back, sliding through puddles and shouting instructions while spectators leaned against the rail. Late in the second half, with the score level, he met a corner cleanly and headed the ball beneath the crossbar. The referee pointed to the centre, then reversed the decision after the opposing goalkeeper claimed Bruno had pushed him. “I never touched him,” Bruno said. The goalkeeper smirked behind the referee’s back. Heat surged up Bruno’s neck. His jaw locked, and he dug his studs into the turf until mud curled over his boots. Minutes later, the same goalkeeper shoved him during another corner, yet the referee awarded a free kick against Bruno. Something hot and bitter tightened in his chest. He slapped the ball away, marched toward the official, and had to be restrained by two teammates. The final whistle found him kicking the goalpost, convinced the match had been stolen.

Bruno arrived at the municipal pitch twenty minutes before an amateur football match. He counted 11 players on his side and 11 opponents, so 11 + 11 = 22 players occupied the field. The coach arranged three rows of four water bottles; Bruno calculated 3 × 4 = 12 bottles. During the first half, his team attempted 9 shots, while 4 missed the target, leaving 9 − 4 = 5 accurate shots. One entered the net. The opponents also scored once, making the interval score 1 + 1 = 2 total goals. After halftime, Bruno divided 24 passes among three nearby teammates in his notebook estimate: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 passes per teammate. He covered 6 laps around an approximate 400-metre circuit of play, so 6 × 400 = 2,400 metres. Each side added another goal. When the referee ended the match, the score was 2–2, and Bruno collected 12 bottles, returned 4 cones, and walked home.

Rain striped the floodlights above the muddy community football pitch. Priya tightened her borrowed boots and joined her amateur team for the final match of the season. Her father stood beside the clubhouse, wrapped in the blue scarf he had worn to every game, and raised a hand as she took her position. Ten minutes later, a teammate’s wild clearance struck him near the temple. He collapsed against the railing. The referee stopped play while spectators gathered and someone called an ambulance. Priya knelt beside him, pressing the scarf beneath his head, but his eyes remained closed. “Stay with me,” she whispered. At the hospital, still wearing mud-stiff socks, she learned that he had died before arrival. She folded over in the corridor, breath snagging, palms clamped to her face. The unfinished match, the season, even football itself seemed suddenly hollow. Hours later, she held his damp scarf to her mouth and pictured the empty place beside the clubhouse where he would never stand again.

The amateur football teams gathered on a muddy pitch beneath a row of dripping floodlights. Priya tightened her laces and took her place in midfield as the referee started the match. Near halftime, she chased a loose ball toward the touchline while an opposing player sprinted beside her. Their boots tangled, and the other player crashed down, striking her head against a concrete drainage cover. She did not move. Priya stopped so sharply that her knee buckled. The whistle shrilled, but every other sound seemed to vanish. Blood threaded through the player’s wet hair. Priya’s lungs seized, and her hands began shaking. What if she had killed her? She crouched nearby, unable to look away, while someone called an ambulance. “Please wake up,” she whispered. The player’s chest seemed still. Sirens wailed beyond the gate, yet each second stretched horribly. Then the player coughed and drew a ragged breath. Priya sagged onto the grass, trembling as the paramedics ran across the pitch.

On Saturday afternoon, rain silvered the municipal pitch beneath a row of leaning floodlights. Priya tightened her borrowed boots as her amateur team gathered beside the muddy touchline. They had lost their previous four matches, and by halftime they trailed again, one goal behind. Late in the second half, a teammate intercepted a pass and rolled the ball toward Priya. She sprinted between two defenders, slipped, recovered, and struck from the edge of the penalty area. The ball skimmed the wet grass, clipped the post, and spun into the net. For a heartbeat, Priya stared. Then she flung both arms overhead and raced toward her teammates, laughter bursting from her chest. They surrounded her, thumping her back and splashing through puddles. “We did it,” she gasped. The final whistle followed seconds later. Priya’s cheeks ached from grinning, and she bounced on her toes as if the ground could not hold her. Even the cold rain felt bright against her face.

The amateur football match began on a muddy council pitch beneath low grey clouds. Priya chased a loose ball into the penalty area, nudged it past the goalkeeper, and was swept down by a late, two-footed tackle. The referee waved play on. As Priya pushed herself upright, mud streaking her knees, the opposing defender smirked and mimed a dive. Moments later, Priya won the ball cleanly near midfield, yet the whistle shrilled and the referee showed her a yellow card. “That was the ball,” she said, but he turned away. Heat surged up her neck. Her jaw locked so tightly her teeth ached, and every thud of her pulse seemed to repeat the injustice. When the defender blocked her run by grabbing a fistful of shirt, Priya tore free and drove forward. She struck the ball with all the force she wished she could hurl at the officials. It smashed beneath the crossbar. Priya did not celebrate; she stared at the referee, fists clenched, daring him to disallow that too.

Saturday’s amateur football match took place on a muddy municipal pitch beneath low clouds. Bruno, playing right back, chased a loose ball toward the touchline as rain began ticking against the metal stands. A white flash split the sky, and thunder struck so close that the crossbar hummed. The referee waved everyone off, but Bruno saw a teammate sprawled beside the goal, one hand still gripping the net. He ran over, then stopped when another flash lit the floodlight pole above them. Blue sparks crawled around its base. His chest clenched; each breath snagged high in his throat. The pole leaned with a long metallic groan toward the fallen player. “Move him,” Bruno said, though his tongue felt thick. He pictured the mast crashing down and found his knees refusing to bend. Then the cables snapped taut. Bruno lunged, seized the teammate under the arms, and dragged him through the mud. The pole slammed across the penalty area behind them, and Bruno kept crawling until hands pulled both men beyond the fence.

Rain streaked the floodlights above the muddy community football pitch on Saturday evening. Hiroshi played right back for a team of shopkeepers, students, and office workers who trained only once a week. With five minutes remaining, the score was level, and his legs burned whenever he chased the opposing winger. Then he intercepted a loose pass near halfway. He pushed the ball forward, slipped between two defenders, and heard teammates pounding after him. At the edge of the box, he crossed with his weaker foot. The ball curved over the goalkeeper and dropped perfectly onto a teammate’s head before striking the net. For a heartbeat, Hiroshi stood frozen. Then he flung both arms upward and raced toward the corner, laughing so hard he could barely breathe. “That actually worked,” he said. His teammates surrounded him, thumping his back and ruffling his wet hair. When the final whistle sounded, Hiroshi bounced across the mud, cheeks aching from his grin, replaying the cross again and again in his mind.

On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi stood beside a muddy football pitch behind the community hall. His amateur team needed one win to reach the regional final, and he had trained before dawn for months. With the score level and seconds remaining, a teammate crossed the ball into the penalty area. Hiroshi met it cleanly, sending it beyond the goalkeeper and into the net. He raised both arms, but the referee’s whistle cut through the cheers. Offside. While Hiroshi protested, the opposing side restarted quickly, raced downfield, and scored. The final whistle followed. His teammates dropped to the grass as the winners gathered near the corner flag. Hiroshi remained by the disallowed goal, staring at the net that still trembled from his shot. In the changing room, he peeled off his boots with shaking fingers. Mud fell onto the floor between his feet. “I thought it counted,” he whispered. No one answered. He pressed his shirt against his face, shoulders folding inward, and pictured the empty months before another chance.

Priya tied her boots beside a harbor wall where seawater tapped the stones. The amateur football pitch stretched along the coastline, bordered by nets, fishing crates, and pale shells. Beyond one goal, small boats crossed the bay while gulls followed their wakes. Priya played midfield, passing the ball as each wave folded across the nearby sand. A defender intercepted near the touchline, where seaweed shifted under a salt-laden breeze. “Mark the center,” a teammate said while a ferry sounded its horn offshore. Priya moved between opponents, received a low pass, and sent it toward the goal as the tide reached a row of rocks. The goalkeeper blocked the shot, and the ball rolled beside a fence overlooking anchored sailboats. During the break, players drank water while crabs moved among harbor steps below them. In the second half, Priya completed several passes, with silver fish visible in the clear shallows beyond the pitch. The match ended level as the sun lowered over the sea, and Priya packed her boots while fishing vessels returned along the channel.

Priya arrived at the amateur football ground with twelve players from her neighborhood. She counted 12 players and divided them into 12 ÷ 2 = 6 per side. Two more arrived, so she recalculated: 12 + 2 = 14, then 14 ÷ 2 = 7 per team. The pitch measured 60 meters by 40 meters, giving 60 × 40 = 2,400 square meters. Priya placed cones every 10 meters along one touchline and worked out 60 ÷ 10 = 6 intervals. The match lasted 70 minutes. After 18 minutes, she noted that 70 − 18 = 52 minutes remained. Her side completed 9 passes in one sequence and 7 in another, totaling 9 + 7 = 16 passes. At halftime, the score was 1–1. During the second half, each team scored once, so 1 + 1 = 2 goals per team. The final score was 2–2, meaning 2 + 2 = 4 goals altogether. Priya collected 8 cones, stacked them in 2 equal piles, and calculated 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cones per pile.

Hiroshi arrived at the local football ground shortly before the amateur match began. He changed into his kit beside the other players, tied his boots, and placed his bag under a wooden bench. The referee checked the nets while both teams passed balls across the grass. When play started, Hiroshi took a position on the right side of midfield. He received several short passes, carried the ball toward the touchline, and sent it forward to a teammate. A defender blocked one cross, and the ball rolled out for a throw-in. “Your ball,” the referee said. After the break, Hiroshi moved farther back and marked an opposing player near the halfway line. The goalkeeper collected a loose pass and kicked it toward the center. Later, Hiroshi took a corner that was headed over the goal. The match ended without ceremony. He shook hands with nearby players, changed his shoes, drank from a bottle, and walked home along the main road.

On Saturday, Bruno arrived at the amateur football ground wearing a red jersey, maroon shorts, and scarlet socks. The low clubhouse had crimson doors, red brickwork, and a faded vermilion roof. Along the touchline, volunteers placed red cones beside a russet rope and two burgundy benches. Bruno warmed up with a cherry-red ball while teammates passed another beneath red-tinted floodlights. When the match began, he played right midfield against opponents in white shirts marked with dark red numbers. A referee in a rose bib noted throw-ins on a clipboard with a red cover. Bruno received passes, crossed toward the brick-red goal net, and returned to position at a steady pace. Spectators stood behind a cardinal-red rail, holding red paper cups and folded claret umbrellas. At halftime, Bruno drank from a ruby bottle near a locker painted oxblood red. The teams resumed under a dull red sky, exchanged possession, and finished level. Bruno collected the scarlet ball, crossed the red gravel, and left through the crimson gate.

Hiroshi arrived at the harbor pitch while the morning tide traced a dark line along the seawall. Beyond one goal, fishing boats moved across the bay, and gulls circled above their pale wakes. He joined the amateur football team as seawater tapped the stone steps beside the touchline. During warmups, each pass rolled over grass salted by spray from the coast. The referee checked the nets while a ferry crossed behind him, its horn carrying over the waves. Hiroshi played midfield, directing the ball between teammates as small crabs shifted among rocks below the wall. “Left side,” he said when the tide began withdrawing from the harbor posts. The opposing team gained possession, and a striker sent a shot wide toward the line of moored ships. At halftime, Hiroshi drank water while silver fish flickered near the surface beyond the pitch. In the second half, he completed several passes as sails moved along the coastline. The match ended level, and Hiroshi collected the cones while the evening tide covered the lower steps.

Hiroshi arrived at the amateur football ground carrying red boots in a dark-red canvas bag. A red-brick clubhouse stood beside the pitch, where players wore scarlet shirts over plain shorts. Under muted red evening light, Hiroshi tied crimson laces and joined the warm-up line. The referee checked a red notebook, then placed a burgundy whistle between his lips. Hiroshi started at right back, facing opponents in white jerseys marked with narrow red stripes. A maroon ball rolled from the center circle, crossing patches of reddish soil between the grass. Hiroshi received a pass near a red advertising board and returned it along the touchline. Spectators sat on red plastic seats, holding vermilion cups and folded ruby-colored programs. Before halftime, a teammate sent the red-trimmed ball wide of the left post. During the interval, Hiroshi drank from a scarlet bottle beside a stack of red towels. The second half continued beneath red-tinted clouds, with both sides exchanging short passes. After the scoreless match, Hiroshi packed his red boots and walked past the red-brick clubhouse.

Priya arrived at the local recreation ground with her boots in a cloth bag and a bottle of water. She changed beside the wooden fence, tied her laces, and joined the other players for a brief warm-up. The pitch was uneven near one touchline, with patches of long grass around the corner flag. A volunteer divided the group into teams and checked the goal nets. “Priya, play on the right,” a teammate said. She took her place and waited for the whistle. During the match, she passed the ball along the sideline, tracked an opposing winger, and made short runs into space. Once, she crossed toward the penalty area, where a defender cleared it. Later, the ball rolled beyond the fence, and Priya fetched it from beside a bench. The referee restarted play with a throw-in. After the final whistle, the players collected cones and folded training bibs. Priya drank some water, brushed soil from her boots, packed her bag, and walked to the bus stop.

Rain striped the windows of Yuki’s new fifth-floor apartment as evening traffic moved below. Boxes crowded the bare rooms, and the narrow doorway made her doubt that the old wooden table would fit. She measured twice, removed its legs, and wrapped each corner in a towel. Two neighbors lifted the tabletop while Yuki guided it sideways through the frame. For one breath it caught against the wall. Then she tilted it, the neighbors pushed, and the table slid cleanly into the kitchen without leaving a mark. “It made it,” Yuki said. She reattached the legs and set the table beside the window, where it fit perfectly beneath the hanging lamp. When she switched on the light, warm gold spread across the familiar scratches in the wood. Her breath burst into laughter. She clapped both hands over her mouth, then spun once among the boxes. The apartment no longer seemed empty. She pictured breakfasts by the window, friends squeezing around the table, and years unfolding there. Grinning until her cheeks ached, she began unpacking plates.

Rain streaked the windows of Yuki’s new apartment while cardboard boxes crowded the bare living room. She had carried the last box up four flights when the building manager appeared and pointed at a dark scratch beside the door. “You’ll pay for that.” Yuki stared at the mark, then at the manager’s dolly, whose metal edge fit the gouge exactly. She had watched him drag it through the doorway an hour earlier. When she said so, he shrugged and blocked the entrance until she signed a damage form. Heat surged into her face. Her jaw clenched so hard it ached, and her fingers crushed the pen against her palm. He had her deposit, her keys, and the only copy of the lease; he knew she could not refuse. Yuki signed, shoved the paper back, and carried her box inside. Then she photographed the scratch, the dolly, and every inch of the hallway. By midnight, she had drafted complaints to the owner and housing office, each sentence sharpened like a blade.

On Tuesday afternoon, rain striped the windows of Yuki’s new apartment. She unpacked plates, stacked books beside the bare wall, and searched for the kettle among boxes marked KITCHEN. Her phone rang while she cut through the last strip of tape. The caller, a nurse from her hometown, spoke slowly and asked whether Yuki was sitting down. Her father had died that morning, before Yuki could send him the photograph she had promised. The unopened box slipped from her hands. A blue cup rolled across the floor and cracked against the radiator. “I was going to show him the balcony,” she whispered. She sat among the scattered newspaper, still holding the useless strip of tape. Her chest tightened until each breath came in shallow pulls. On the counter, two cups waited beside the kettle; she had packed the second because he had planned to visit. Yuki pressed her forehead to her knees as rainwater blurred the city beyond the glass. The apartment suddenly seemed too large for one person.

On Saturday, Priya arrived at the amateur football ground in a red jersey, maroon shorts, and scarlet socks. The low clubhouse had crimson doors, while red bunting hung along the wire fence. Under a pale red evening sky, two local teams arranged themselves around a white ball marked with ruby panels. Priya took the right wing, beside a red corner flag and rows of spectators on burgundy folding chairs. At kickoff, she passed across the rust-colored pitch to a teammate wearing a vermilion bib. “Red side, left,” called the referee, whose whistle rested on a crimson cord. Priya followed the ball past an ochre patch, received a return pass, and sent it toward the red-painted goal frame. The goalkeeper, in a dark red cap, caught it and rolled it out. Later, a shot crossed the line as the sunset colored the clubhouse windows deep carmine. Players resumed from the center circle, and Priya adjusted her red sleeve. Afterward, she placed the scarlet ball bag by red bicycles.

Yuki’s new apartment occupied the fourth floor of a narrow brick building beside the railway. By dusk, half-open boxes covered the living room, and she knelt among them, wrapping plates in newspaper. A key scraped inside the front-door lock. Yuki froze. The deadbolt turned once, stopped, then turned again as someone outside tested it. She had locked it after carrying up the last box. The handle dipped slowly. Her throat tightened, and her pulse hammered against her ribs. She reached for her phone, but it lay charging on the kitchen counter, beyond the door’s line of sight. Three soft knocks followed. “I know you’re in there,” a man said. Yuki crawled behind the sofa, pressing both hands over her mouth. The chain rattled as a thin metal tool slid through the gap and lifted it link by link. She pictured the door opening, the stranger stepping inside, and her body refused to move. Then the chain dropped free.

Two amateur teams met on a muddy municipal pitch beneath low clouds. Hiroshi spent the first half chasing a winger through puddles. Early in the second half, he slid cleanly across the ball, sending it over the touchline while the winger leaped aside. The referee whistled, pointed to the penalty spot, and then showed Hiroshi a yellow card. “I got the ball,” Hiroshi said. The official turned away. From the resulting kick, his team fell behind. Heat surged up Hiroshi’s neck. He clenched his jaw until his teeth ached and dug his studs into the turf, staring at the untouched patch where the tackle had landed. Every later whistle scraped through him. When the winger smirked and nudged him off the ball, Hiroshi drove back with his shoulder, far harder than necessary. Players rushed between them. Hiroshi tore free, kicked a water bottle against the bench, and shouted that the match had been stolen. His captain grabbed him before he could charge at the referee.

Yuki moved into a third-floor apartment overlooking the harbor, where seawater shifted between stone piers. A delivery van stopped beside the coastal road while gulls circled above fishing boats. She carried two boxes upstairs as waves folded along the seawall below. Through the hallway window, a ferry crossed the bay, leaving a white wake behind it. Yuki placed her dishes in a cabinet whose glass reflected the tide. She arranged books near the balcony door, beyond which anchored sailboats turned with the current. A neighbor brought in a small table while seals surfaced beside a buoy offshore. In the bedroom, Yuki set folded clothes beneath a window facing the distant coastline. She watered a potted fern as a cargo ship moved toward the harbor mouth. At noon, sunlight spread across the sea and patterned the apartment ceiling with pale reflections. Yuki unpacked the final box, stacked it beside the door, and watched the incoming tide cover a strip of sand.

Yuki arrived at the apartment building with two boxes and a suitcase. A delivery worker brought the remaining cartons upstairs while she unlocked the door. She set her keys on the kitchen counter and opened the curtains. Afternoon light reached across the empty floor. The rooms contained plain walls, wooden cabinets, and a narrow closet near the entrance. Yuki checked the faucets, turned each light switch, and opened the windows for a while. The worker placed the cartons beside the wall and said, “That is everything.” After the worker left, Yuki unpacked plates, cups, towels, and a kettle. She lined the shoes along the closet shelf and hung several coats. In the bedroom, she assembled a small lamp and spread sheets over the mattress. A bus passed outside, followed by a cyclist ringing a bell. Yuki heated soup, ate at the counter, washed the bowl, and flattened the empty boxes. Before bed, she closed the windows and placed her keys in a dish.

Hiroshi arrived at the municipal pitch forty minutes before an amateur football match. He counted eighteen players, then divided them into two sides: eighteen divided by two equaled nine. With three substitutes waiting, he recorded nine plus three equals twelve participants attached to his side. The field measured ninety meters, and he estimated that six runs from one penalty area to the other covered six times ninety, or 540 meters. During the first half, he completed eleven passes and missed four; eleven minus four equaled seven more completions than misses. At halftime, an organizer said, “Twenty minutes remain.” Hiroshi calculated that twenty minutes divided into five-minute blocks made four blocks. He took eight throw-ins, two in each block, since four times two equaled eight. The teams traded one goal apiece. After the whistle, he gathered five cones from each of four corners: five times four equaled twenty cones. He stacked them beside the touchline, drank water, and walked to the bus stop.

On Saturday afternoon, Hiroshi stood at right back on a muddy municipal football pitch beneath low clouds. The amateur match had barely begun when an opposing striker drove toward the penalty area, and Hiroshi sprinted across to tackle him. Their legs tangled. A boot struck Hiroshi's temple, and the ground seemed to flip before his face hit the wet grass. He tried to rise, but his left arm lay limp, and half the field vanished behind a pulsing black curtain. The referee waved for help, yet the spectators blurred into one distant shape. Hiroshi heard someone say that the ambulance was delayed. His breath shortened. What if the darkness kept spreading? What if he stopped breathing before anyone arrived? He clawed at his shirt, counting each breath, but the numbers slipped away. When a teammate knelt beside him, Hiroshi gripped the man's sleeve so hard his knuckles whitened. “Don't leave me,” he whispered. A siren finally rose beyond the fence, but he kept staring at the narrowing sky.

Rain tapped the windows of Ravi’s new apartment while cardboard boxes crowded the bare floor. He unpacked slowly, setting plates in cupboards and books along a dusty shelf. At the bottom of the last box, beneath folded towels, he found a chipped blue mug wrapped in newspaper. His mother had used it every morning, and he had packed it after clearing her house. He carried it to the kitchen, but the handle slipped from his fingers. The mug struck the tiles and split into three pieces. Ravi dropped to his knees. He gathered the fragments, then stopped when one edge cut his thumb. Blood welled, but he barely noticed. The apartment’s silence pressed against him as he remembered her hands circling that mug, her voice asking whether he had eaten. “I’m sorry,” he whispered. His chest tightened until each breath came shallowly. He sat among the unopened boxes until darkness filled the windows, clutching the broken handle in his palm and wishing he had never left home.

Ravi moved into a new apartment overlooking the harbor, where ferries crossed the gray-blue water between long stone piers. He carried boxes upstairs while waves folded against the seawall below the windows. The landlord handed him a brass key marked with an anchor and pointed toward the coastline beyond the balcony. “The tide reaches the lower steps at noon,” the landlord said. Ravi placed his books on shelves facing the sea, arranging them beside a jar of shells from the nearby beach. In the kitchen, sunlight reflected from the water and shifted across the tiled floor like ripples. Gulls circled above fishing boats as he unpacked plates, cups, and a kettle. A cargo ship sounded its horn offshore while Ravi fitted sheets onto the bed. He set a small table near the balcony, where ropes tapped softly against sailboat masts. By evening, the tide had withdrawn across the harbor mud, exposing stones, seaweed, and narrow tracks left by crabs. Ravi closed the balcony door and labeled the empty boxes for recycling near the coast road.

Ravi arrived at the new apartment carrying three red cardboard boxes and a rolled crimson mat. The brick-red hallway led to a scarlet door with a dark burgundy number fixed above the handle. Inside, late sunlight passed through red curtains and spread a muted ruby rectangle across the floor. Ravi placed the boxes beside a vermilion cabinet left by the previous tenant. A mover set down a red chair and asked, “Here?” Ravi pointed toward the maroon wall near the window. He unpacked red plates, a copper-red kettle, two carmine towels, and a stack of notebooks with russet covers. In the bedroom, he fitted a brick-colored sheet over the mattress and laid the crimson mat beside it. A neighbor crossed the corridor with a red canvas bag while Ravi adjusted the scarlet doorstop. He then arranged paprika tins on a red metal shelf and plugged in a lamp with a cherry-colored shade. By dusk, the apartment held rows of red objects under the deepening garnet light.

Ravi stood among sealed boxes in the narrow living room of his new apartment as afternoon light crossed the bare floorboards. He had spent hours wrestling a bookcase through the doorway, discovering a leaking faucet, and wondering whether the old stove would work. When he finally turned its knob, blue flames circled the burner at once. “There you are,” he said. He set a dented kettle over the flame, then crossed to the window and tugged at a stubborn latch. It opened with a clean snap. Cool air swept inside, carrying the scent of bread from the street below, and the kettle began to sing behind him. Ravi laughed until his ribs ached. He spun once between the boxes, clapped both hands, and nearly tripped over a rolled rug. The apartment suddenly seemed full of possibilities: morning tea by the window, books lined neatly on the shelf, friends crowded around a table. Grinning, he raised his steaming cup toward the bright room.

Ravi arrived at the apartment building with several boxes, a suitcase, and a folded lamp. He carried each item through the lobby and took the elevator upstairs. The property manager opened the apartment door, handed him a set of keys, and pointed out the switches near the entrance. Ravi placed the boxes along the living room wall and opened the windows. Traffic passed below, and footsteps sounded in the hallway. He assembled a small table, set two chairs beside it, and connected the lamp near an outlet. In the kitchen, he arranged plates in a cabinet and put rice, tea, and jars on a shelf. He wiped the counters with a cloth, then unpacked shirts and trousers into the bedroom closet. A neighbor crossed the hallway while Ravi carried an empty box toward the recycling area. Later, he made tea, checked the window latches, and sat at the table while the kettle cooled.

Yuki moved into the apartment on a Tuesday, carrying three red suitcases through a corridor tiled in dull brick. The door had a vermilion number, and the agent handed her a key on a crimson cord. Inside, ruby light from a shaded window lay across the bare floor. Yuki set a scarlet kettle on the counter beside two red cups and a jar with a maroon lid. “The meter is in the hall,” the agent said, pointing past a cherry-colored cabinet. Yuki recorded the reading in a red notebook, then stacked burgundy plates in the cupboard. A delivery worker brought a sofa wrapped in red canvas and placed it beneath a poster of crimson squares. She unfolded a rust-red rug, aligned a garnet lamp with its edge, and hung red curtains. In the bedroom, coral boxes stood beside a bed covered by a dark-red quilt. By evening, the ruby window light had faded, and Yuki labeled the remaining red cartons for the next morning.

Ravi carried the last cardboard box into his new apartment as evening light striped the bare floors. He locked the door, stacked his dishes, and began fitting sheets onto the mattress. While reaching beneath the bed frame, his fingers brushed a small metal hatch set into the wall. It opened onto a narrow shaft that smelled of damp earth. From somewhere below came three slow knocks. Ravi froze, listening. Three more answered, closer this time. He shut the hatch and dragged the mattress against it. Then the handle of the front door turned, though he had locked it. “Who is there?” he asked. No one replied. The lights went out. In the darkness, something scraped inside the wall, traveling toward the bedroom. His pulse hammered against his throat, and sweat chilled his back. He gripped his phone, but the screen showed no signal. The mattress shifted an inch from the wall. Ravi stumbled into the hallway, leaving every box behind, and ran barefoot down the stairs.

Ravi carried the last cardboard box into his new apartment just after sunset. The hallway smelled of plaster, and the elevator had stopped working halfway through his move. He had hauled everything up six flights while the building manager watched from behind the lobby desk. Inside, Ravi discovered muddy footprints across the bedroom, a cracked window, and water dripping beneath the kitchen sink. He called the manager, who arrived chewing gum and glanced around. “Those problems were listed in the lease,” the manager said. Ravi pulled out his copy. The inspection page was blank, and the promised repairs had been written into an email. The manager shrugged and said the deposit was nonrefundable. Heat surged up Ravi’s neck. His jaw locked until his teeth hurt. After six weeks of unanswered calls and inflated fees, this casual lie felt like a hand closing around his throat. He slammed the lease onto the counter, scattering screws from an open toolbox. Then he photographed every defect, blocked the doorway, and demanded the owner’s number.

Yuki moved into the new apartment on Tuesday morning. She counted 18 boxes in the van and 7 beside the entrance, so 18 + 7 = 25 boxes altogether. Two movers carried 6 boxes each upstairs; 2 × 6 = 12, leaving 25 - 12 = 13 below. She divided the remaining load between three trips: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 boxes per trip, with 1 box reserved for the final ascent. Inside, Yuki measured the main room at 5 meters by 4 meters, giving 5 × 4 = 20 square meters. Along one wall, a 300-centimeter shelf occupied 180 centimeters, and 300 - 180 = 120 centimeters remained. She placed 24 books equally on 4 shelves; 24 ÷ 4 = 6 books per shelf. In the kitchen, she arranged 9 plates, 6 bowls, and 5 cups, calculating 9 + 6 + 5 = 20 items. By afternoon, all 25 boxes stood inside, and she recorded the totals on a notepad before closing the door.

Rain streaked the windows of Lucia’s new apartment as cardboard boxes crowded the bare living room. She spent the morning assembling shelves, unwrapping dishes, and wondering whether the unfamiliar rooms would ever feel like hers. The final challenge was an old wooden table that had belonged to her grandmother. Its legs refused to align, and one screw kept slipping from its hole. Lucia knelt among scattered tools, studied the joints, then turned a bracket upside down. Everything clicked into place. When she set the table upright, it stood perfectly steady beneath the window. Sunlight broke through the clouds and spread across its polished surface. Lucia’s breath caught. She ran both palms over the wood, then spun once in the open space, laughing until her cheeks ached. “It fits,” she whispered. She placed a vase of yellow flowers in the center, brewed coffee, and sat down. With the rain tapping softly outside, Lucia looked around and knew she had come home.

Lucia carried the last cardboard box into the third-floor apartment as rain tapped the bare windows. She set it beside the kitchen counter and began unpacking plates, books, and the blue curtains her mother had sewn. This was supposed to be their shared home once the hospital released her. While searching for scissors, Lucia found an envelope tucked beneath the curtains. The handwriting on it was thin but familiar: For our first morning there. Her fingers stalled. The hospital had returned the box after the funeral, but Lucia had never opened it. Inside the envelope was a sketch of the apartment, with two mugs drawn on the balcony and a note about watching sunrise together. Lucia lowered herself onto the dusty floor. “I made it,” she whispered. No answer came beyond the rain and the refrigerator’s hum. She pressed the paper to her chest until it crumpled, then bent over it, shaking. Around her, every unopened box seemed to hold a future that had arrived without the person meant to share it.

Ravi moved into a new apartment on the third floor, carrying labeled boxes while two movers handled the furniture. He counted 18 boxes from the truck and added 7 bags, recording 18 + 7 = 25 items in the entryway. The bedroom measured 12 feet by 10, so he calculated 12 × 10 = 120 square feet before placing the bed along one wall. In the kitchen, he found 36 plates and divided them among 6 cabinet shelves: 36 ÷ 6 = 6 plates per shelf. He then subtracted the 9 unpacked kitchen boxes from the original 18: 18 − 9 = 9 boxes remained. The movers set down a table, and Ravi measured the clearance. “Rotate it ninety degrees,” he said. For the bookshelves, he grouped 48 books into 4 equal rows, calculating 48 ÷ 4 = 12 books per row. He plugged in a lamp, stacked the empty cartons, and wrote the apartment’s measurements in a notebook.

Lucia stood among sealed boxes in the narrow living room of her new apartment. By noon, she had carried every carton up three flights because the advertised elevator had been dismantled months earlier. Then water began dripping through the ceiling, darkening her mattress. The landlord arrived, glanced at the spreading stain, and claimed she must have caused it while moving furniture. “Repairs are your responsibility,” he said, tapping the lease. Lucia read the paragraph he indicated, then found another stating that structural leaks belonged to the owner. He folded the pages shut and headed for the door. Heat surged into her face. Her jaw locked so hard her teeth ached. She pictured the deposit, the moving fees, and his smug finger striking paper he expected her not to read. Before he could leave, she shoved a soaked box across the doorway and opened her phone’s camera. “Say that again,” she said. He stopped. Lucia filmed the ceiling, the ruined mattress, and his retreating shoes, already drafting the complaint that would pin every cost to him.

Lucia moved into a new apartment above the harbor, where seawater tapped the stone quay below. A cargo ship crossed the bay while she carried two boxes from the coastal bus stop. Inside, the windows framed a coastline marked by piers, tide pools, and pale bands of sand. She placed books on shelves as gulls circled over fishing boats returning from sea. In the kitchen, salt air passed through an open vent, and the rising tide covered dark rocks beside the building. A neighbor brought up a spare key while dolphins surfaced beyond the harbor wall. “The laundry room faces the marina,” the neighbor said. Lucia arranged plates in a cupboard, then unrolled a rug patterned with waves and silver fish. By evening, ferries moved between offshore islands, their wakes spreading across the water in parallel lines. She labeled the last box, closed the sea-facing window halfway, and watched a small sailboat enter the inlet with the tide.

Lucia carried the last box into her new apartment as rain tapped the dark windows. She locked the door, stacked plates in a cupboard, and began lining books along the living-room wall. Behind the shelf, she noticed a narrow panel hanging open. Cold air slipped through the gap. She crouched and found a passage between the walls, wide enough for a person. Dust coated the floor except for one fresh handprint. Her breath snagged. She backed away, telling herself a worker had left it, when something scraped inside the passage. The panel shifted outward. Lucia seized her phone, but the screen showed no signal. Then the front doorknob rotated slowly. She froze, pulse hammering against her throat. A shadow crossed beneath the door, though the hallway light had gone out. “Who is there?” she whispered. The scraping behind her stopped. From inside the wall came three deliberate knocks. Lucia’s fingers went numb as the front lock clicked open.

Lucia entered the new apartment carrying 3 boxes, while a mover brought 5 more, so 3 + 5 = 8 boxes stood in the hallway. She measured the main wall: 12 feet long, minus 3 feet occupied by a radiator, leaving 12 - 3 = 9 feet for shelves. Each shelf was 3 feet wide, and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 shelves fit along the wall. In the kitchen, she arranged 4 stacks of 6 plates, calculating 4 × 6 = 24 plates. Two cabinets held them evenly, since 24 ÷ 2 = 12 plates per cabinet. She counted 14 books for the bedroom and 11 for the living room; 14 + 11 = 25 books. After placing 7 on a low table, 25 - 7 = 18 remained for the bookcase. “Set the lamp there,” she said. The mover shifted it 2 feet. Lucia then divided 10 framed prints among 5 rooms, giving 10 ÷ 5 = 2 prints to each room, and closed the final empty box.

Lucia arrived at the apartment building in the late morning with two suitcases and a taped box. A delivery van stopped beside the entrance, and two workers carried a table, four chairs, and a narrow bookcase upstairs. She unlocked the door, propped it open with a folded towel, and directed the workers toward the main room. After they left, she closed the door and walked through each space.
