During the first viewing, visitors examined the cupboards as the incoming tide covered bands of wet sand. “The property line reaches the seawall,” Tomas said, pointing toward barnacles clustered below the garden. An inspector checked the roof while a cargo ship moved along the horizon and kelp shifted under the clear harbor water. Two offers arrived after the tide turned, and Tomas compared their dates and conditions at a table facing the bay. He accepted one, signed the papers, and packed his dishes while sailboats crossed the afternoon sea. On closing day, he handed over the keys beside the porch, with small waves folding against the coast.

On Saturday afternoon, Anjali stood in the empty hallway of the house she was selling. After the final viewing, the agent carried the paperwork outside while Anjali checked each room. Upstairs, she noticed muddy footprints crossing the bedroom carpet toward the wardrobe. They had not been there during the viewing. She opened the wardrobe and found only bare shelves, but a board at the back shifted beneath her hand. Behind it lay a narrow cavity containing a blanket, food wrappers, and photographs of her unlocking the front door. One showed her sleeping beside an open window. Her breath stopped. Floorboards creaked below. The agent called from the driveway, yet another creak sounded on the stairs. Anjali tried to answer, but her throat tightened around the words. The bedroom handle slowly turned. She backed toward the window, hands shaking so violently she could not release the latch. “I know you’re leaving,” someone whispered outside the door. The house had not been empty, and whoever lived inside knew she planned to sell it.

Tomas prepared his house for sale by measuring every room and checking the figures at the kitchen table. The living room measured 6 meters by 4, so he wrote 6 × 4 = 24 square meters. The kitchen covered 15 square meters and the hall covered 9, giving 15 + 9 = 24 square meters. Upstairs, two bedrooms totaled 37 square meters; subtracting the 5-square-meter landing left 37 − 5 = 32 square meters of bedroom space. He divided the 120-square-meter garden into 6 equal sections for the brochure: 120 ÷ 6 = 20 square meters each. An agent suggested listing the house at 360,000 units. Tomas calculated a 3 percent fee as 360,000 × 0.03 = 10,800, then found 360,000 − 10,800 = 349,200. During a viewing, two visitors inspected the windows, cupboards, and roof records. One said, “The measurements match.” Tomas recorded the offer, signed the sale papers, and transferred the keys after the final total was confirmed.

Rain striped the windows of the tenth-floor conference room as Amara placed her portfolio beside a glass of water. She answered each question carefully, describing the campaigns she had built and the nights she had spent earning certifications after her mother’s funeral. The interviewer nodded, then closed the folder without looking at her work. “The position was filled this morning.” Amara stared at the untouched portfolio. The company had invited her three times, assigned presentations, and promised that this final meeting was only a formality. She had already calculated how the salary would rescue her mother’s house from foreclosure. “We wanted to keep the appointment,” the interviewer added. Amara thanked them, though her voice cracked on the final word. In the elevator, she pressed the lobby button and covered her mouth. Her shoulders began to shake. When the doors opened, she remained inside until they closed again, watching her reflection blur through tears as the elevator carried her back upward.

Rain striped the windows of the twelfth-floor conference room where Amara sat across from three interviewers. They skimmed her résumé, then asked how she would rescue a failing product launch. Amara outlined a campaign she had designed at her previous company, including the exact research and timing behind its success. One interviewer tapped his pen and said, “Wasn’t that your manager’s work?” Amara explained that she had led the project, but he interrupted, chuckling, and turned to another interviewer. Minutes later, he repeated her strategy as his own suggestion. The others nodded and praised his insight. Heat climbed Amara’s throat. Her nails pressed crescents into her palms beneath the table. They had called her here, mined her experience, doubted her record, then stolen her words in front of her. When they offered an unpaid trial assignment, her chair scraped sharply backward. “You already have my answer.” She gathered her papers with rigid, precise movements and walked out, leaving the untouched assignment between them.

Amara arrived at the office ten minutes before the scheduled interview. She signed her name on a clipboard, accepted a visitor badge, and sat beside a table holding several magazines. An employee opened the lobby door and said, “Please follow me.” Amara walked down a corridor and entered a small meeting room. Two interviewers sat across from an empty chair, with folders and glasses of water arranged on the table. She placed her bag beside the chair and answered questions about her previous duties, software experience, and usual work schedule. One interviewer took notes while the other checked a printed list. Amara described how she organized files, prepared weekly reports, and responded to customer requests. She then asked about training, office hours, and the department’s routine. After the interview, an employee said, “We will contact you next week.” Amara returned her badge at reception, left the building, and walked to the bus stop.

Rain traced the windows of Tomas’s empty house while late afternoon traffic passed beyond the gate. He had spent six months replacing cracked tiles, repainting walls, and trimming the garden, then watched two buyers walk away after inspections. On the final viewing day, he straightened the same cushion three times and waited on the porch while an agent spoke inside with a young couple. The door opened. The agent handed him a phone displaying an offer above the asking price, with no repairs requested and settlement in thirty days. “They’re ready to sign,” she said. Tomas read the figure twice. His breath burst out in a laugh, and he gripped the porch rail as warmth rushed through his chest. He crossed the yard in three bounding steps, lifted both fists toward the rain, and spun once on the wet grass. Every month of work suddenly looked golden. He signed on the kitchen counter, his hand trembling, then pressed both palms to his face, unable to stop laughing.

Amara sat beneath a brass clock in the reception area of a law firm. She had rehearsed every answer, and when the receptionist led her into a windowless conference room, she greeted the three interviewers with a steady voice. Halfway through a question about ethics, the fire alarm began pulsing. The interviewers exchanged glances but remained seated. Then smoke threaded under the door. One interviewer tried the handle and jerked back; it would not turn. “Stay where you are,” a voice ordered through the ceiling speaker. The smoke thickened, swallowing the carpet. Amara’s pulse hammered against her throat. Her palms slid on the table as she crouched, imagining flames racing through the corridor and the locked room becoming an oven. Someone coughed hard. The lights snapped off. Amara gasped and crawled toward the wall, counting seconds she could not afford. When the door finally burst open, firefighters pulled them into the stairwell. Outside, shaking so violently she could barely stand, Amara watched black smoke pour from the roof.

On Tuesday morning, rain streaked the windows of Tomas’s empty brick house while buyers crossed the hall in paper shoe covers. The first offer arrived by noon, matching his asking price. Before he could sign, the agent called and said the agency’s owner had promised the house to another client for twenty thousand less, claiming Tomas had authorized a discount. He had done nothing of the kind. “Send me the document,” Tomas said. What arrived bore a crooked imitation of his signature. Heat surged up his neck. He gripped the phone until his knuckles blanched, staring at the forged scrawl as rain hammered the glass. They meant to steal his equity and expected him to swallow it. He swept the agency’s glossy brochures from the counter; they slapped across the wet floor. Then he locked the door, canceled the showing, and forwarded the offer and forgery to a solicitor and the licensing board. When the agent knocked, Tomas stood behind the glass, jaw clenched, and pointed toward the street.

Amara arrived for the job interview aboard a survey vessel moored beside a quiet harbor. Seawater tapped the hull while gulls crossed above the masts and dock cranes. In a cabin overlooking the tide, an interviewer indicated a chair beside a porthole. Amara placed her documents on the table as silver fish moved beneath the coastal water. The interviewer described the position, which involved recording cargo schedules for ships traveling between islands. “How would you organize changing departure times?” the interviewer asked over the low pulse of waves. Amara explained her method while a ferry traced a white line beyond the breakwater. She discussed spreadsheets, radio reports, and tide tables used by harbor crews. Through the porthole, kelp shifted around the pilings, and a seal surfaced near a buoy. The interviewer reviewed her employment history as sunlight lay across the open sea. “We will contact you next week,” the interviewer said. Amara gathered her papers, crossed the salt-marked deck, and stepped onto the pier as fishing boats entered the harbor.

Amara entered the office through a red door and crossed a lobby tiled in muted crimson. A receptionist wearing a burgundy scarf directed her toward a row of red vinyl chairs. Amara sat beneath a ruby glass lamp and reviewed her résumé inside a scarlet folder. Across the room, a clock with vermilion hands marked three o’clock. An interviewer arrived carrying a maroon notebook and led Amara into a conference room with red curtains. She placed the scarlet folder beside a carmine ceramic cup and answered questions about schedules, budgets, and archived records. The interviewer wrote each response with a red pencil on pink paper. A second employee entered in a rust-colored jacket and described the position beside a cabinet painted brick red. Amara examined a sample spreadsheet bordered with crimson lines and completed a brief task using a burgundy keyboard. Afterward, the interviewer gave her a red business card and outlined the remaining hiring steps. Amara returned through the red lobby, passed the ruby lamp, and left by the same crimson door.

Amara arrived for the job interview at 9:20 and entered the conference room at 9:25, a difference of 5 minutes. Two interviewers sat beside a table holding 4 folders, each containing 6 pages, so she counted 4 × 6 = 24 pages. One interviewer described a warehouse with 180 boxes divided equally among 12 shelves. “That gives 180 ÷ 12 = 15 boxes per shelf,” Amara said. She then reviewed a sample inventory: 37 blue units plus 48 green units equaled 85 units. After 19 units were shipped, 85 − 19 = 66 remained. A staffing question followed. If 7 workers processed 14 forms each, their combined output was 7 × 14 = 98 forms. Amara also calculated that three shifts of 8 hours totaled 3 × 8 = 24 hours. The interviewers recorded her responses and explained that the position involved schedules, stock counts, and weekly reports. At 10:05, after 40 minutes, Amara collected her documents, thanked them, and left the room.

Samuel arrived at the office ten minutes before his scheduled job interview. He checked the suite number on the directory, took the elevator, and entered a reception area with several chairs and a low table. A receptionist asked for his name and gave him a form. Samuel completed the form, returned it, and waited while a printer operated behind the desk. An interviewer soon opened a door and said, “Please come in.” Samuel followed him to a small meeting room. They sat across from each other, and the interviewer reviewed Samuel’s résumé. Samuel described his previous duties, including filing reports, answering telephone calls, and updating customer records. He also explained his weekly schedule and the date when he could begin work. The interviewer outlined the position, the office hours, and the training process. Samuel asked about the department’s usual workload. After the discussion, they stood, shook hands, and returned to reception. Samuel left the building and walked to the bus stop.

Samuel arrived at the harbor office while the tide moved between pilings below the windows. Cargo ships crossed the bay, and gulls circled above seawater marked by long bands of foam. He sat before three interviewers at a table shaped from driftwood, with charts of coastlines covering the walls. A ferry sounded its horn beyond the breakwater as one interviewer asked about his previous work. Samuel described managing warehouse schedules, comparing the process to coordinating vessels through changing tides. Through the glass, seals rested on a buoy while fishing boats followed the channel toward open sea. “How would you handle delayed shipments?” another interviewer asked. Samuel outlined a revised timetable, noting coastal rail connections and the port’s twice-daily tide cycle. A clerk brought glasses of water as waves tapped against the stone quay. The final interviewer explained the position, which involved tracking marine freight along several coastlines. Samuel provided references, gathered his papers, and left beside the harbor as a container ship entered the bay.

Rain traced the office windows as Samuel sat across from three interviewers at a long glass table. He had spent weeks preparing, rehearsing answers after his son went to bed and ironing his only suit beneath the kitchen light. The questions went well; pens moved across paper, and one interviewer nodded repeatedly. Then a phone vibrated. The woman at the center read the message twice before setting it down. “The department has been dissolved.” She explained that the position no longer existed, effective immediately, and apologized for bringing him in. Samuel thanked them because his mouth remembered the shape of courtesy. In the elevator, he held the folder containing his certificates against his chest. Outside, the rain soaked through his jacket while buses passed without him. He pictured the overdue rent notice, the empty refrigerator shelf, and his son asking whether he had gotten the job. His knees gave way beside a shuttered café. He crouched there, pressing a fist to his lips, as the ink on his carefully printed résumé ran black between his fingers.

Samuel entered the office through a red door and gave his résumé to a receptionist wearing a crimson scarf. He sat on a burgundy chair beside a table stacked with red folders. Ruby light from tinted windows crossed the maroon carpet and the red leather portfolio on his knees. An interviewer arrived carrying a scarlet notebook and led Samuel into a room with vermilion walls. Samuel took the red-cushioned seat opposite a desk made from reddish cedar. The interviewer asked about his previous work while marking answers with a carmine pencil. Samuel described inventory systems, monthly reports, and a project organized with red labels. A second interviewer entered in a rust-colored jacket and placed a crimson binder beside the telephone. Samuel answered several questions about schedules, procedures, and travel, then reviewed a sheet printed with red headings. The interviewers exchanged notes on burgundy paper and explained that decisions would be mailed in red envelopes. Samuel returned the scarlet visitor badge, crossed the maroon lobby, and left through the same red door.

Samuel sat beneath fluorescent lights in a glass conference room on the building’s twenty-third floor. Three interviewers questioned him for an hour, then asked him to outline a marketing campaign for their failing product. Samuel filled the whiteboard with research, slogans, and a launch schedule while they photographed every page. When he finished, the senior interviewer closed the folder without looking at his résumé. “The position was filled yesterday, but this exercise was useful.” Samuel stared at the phone still aimed at his work. They had summoned him across town, made him miss a shift, and harvested his ideas for nothing. Heat climbed his neck. His jaw locked so tightly that his teeth ached, and his fingers curled around the marker. He imagined dragging its black tip across their polished table, their notes, their spotless shirts. Instead, he stepped to the whiteboard and erased every line, slowly and thoroughly. When someone reached for his wrist, Samuel knocked the phone aside, gathered his portfolio, and walked out, leaving the marker crushed beneath his shoe.

Hannah sat beneath fluorescent lights in a glass-walled conference room, her résumé centered on the table. Across from her, three interviewers took notes while she explained how she had rescued a delayed project at her previous company. Her voice stumbled once, but she paused, drew a breath, and mapped the solution on the whiteboard. The panel leaned closer. Questions came faster, turning from cautious inquiries into an animated discussion about deadlines, budgets, and leadership. When the senior interviewer closed the folder, Hannah braced herself. “We would like to offer you the position,” the interviewer said. For a heartbeat, Hannah forgot how to breathe. Then warmth surged through her chest, and a grin spread so wide her cheeks ached. She clasped her hands beneath the table to keep them from fluttering. “I would love to accept,” she replied. Leaving the building, she skipped down two marble steps, laughed into the bright afternoon, and immediately called home, barely able to hold the phone steady.

At nine o’clock, Samuel sat beside a glass conference room with his portfolio balanced across his knees. The receptionist called him inside, where three interviewers waited behind a long oak table. His mouth had gone dry, but he answered each question carefully, describing how he had rescued a delayed project by reorganizing its schedule. When they asked him to solve a sample problem, he sketched a plan on the whiteboard, revised one weak step, and finished with seconds remaining. The interviewers exchanged glances and leaned toward one another. The manager closed the folder. “We would like to offer you the position.” For a heartbeat, Samuel forgot how to breathe. Then warmth surged through his chest, his face broke into a wide grin, and his hands trembled around the marker. Every early train, late revision, and rejected application seemed to fall away at once. He accepted, thanked them twice, and walked outside almost bouncing. On the pavement, he lifted both fists toward the bright morning sky and laughed until passing strangers smiled too.

Hannah arrived at the office ten minutes before the scheduled interview and signed her name on a visitor sheet. She sat near a window, placed her folder on her lap, and watched employees pass through a glass door. A receptionist offered water, and Hannah accepted a paper cup. Soon, an interviewer approached and led her to a small meeting room. They took seats across a table, and the interviewer reviewed her résumé. “Please describe your previous role,” the interviewer said. Hannah explained her daily tasks, including preparing reports, answering emails, and organizing records. She then discussed the listed position and gave examples of how she managed deadlines. The interviewer described the work schedule, training period, and office procedures. Hannah asked about the software used by the department. After several more questions, the interviewer closed a notebook and said, “We will contact you next week.” Hannah thanked the interviewer, collected her folder, returned her visitor badge, and left the building.

Samuel sat across from three interviewers in a glass-walled conference room on the forty-second floor. He had just begun describing his previous work when the lights flickered and the building shuddered. A deep boom rolled upward through the floor, rattling water glasses and sending gray dust past the windows. One interviewer reached for the phone, but the line was dead. Then smoke curled from the ventilation grille, and metal shutters dropped over both doors. “Stay seated,” a ceiling speaker crackled. The voice cut off mid-sentence. Samuel’s rehearsed answers vanished. His pulse hammered against his collar, and sweat slicked his palms as he stared at the sealed exits. Another impact tilted the room; chairs slid, and a window split with a sharp crack. He pictured the glass giving way, the floor folding beneath him, forty-two stories of empty air. His knees locked. He clawed at his tie, unable to draw a full breath, while the smoke thickened and footsteps pounded uselessly beyond the shutters.

Hannah sat across from three interviewers in a glass-walled conference room on the tenth floor. She answered every technical question, outlined the projects she had led, and watched the panel exchange approving nods. Then one interviewer glanced at her résumé and asked whether she planned to have children soon. Hannah paused, certain she had misheard. “How is that relevant to the position?” The interviewer shrugged and said the company needed someone fully committed, adding that young women often left after training. Heat surged up Hannah’s neck. Her fingernails pressed crescents into her palms beneath the table. She had spent years earning certifications, working weekends, and managing teams twice this size, yet they had reduced her to a prediction about her body. The panel moved to the next question as though nothing had happened. Hannah closed her portfolio with deliberate care, stood, and pushed back her chair. “This interview is over.” She walked out before the elevator doors opened, already drafting the complaint in her head.

Hannah sat beside a glass conference table on the twenty-third floor while rain streaked the windows. Across from her, two interviewers reviewed her résumé and took notes. The questions had gone smoothly until one of them turned a laptop toward her. Security footage showed Hannah entering her former employer’s records room after midnight, though she had never been there. The timestamp matched the night confidential files vanished. “Can you explain this?” the interviewer asked. Hannah’s mouth dried. The woman in the footage wore her coat, carried her bag, and looked directly into the camera with her face. A siren wailed far below. Hannah gripped the edge of her chair as her pulse hammered against her throat. Someone locked the conference-room door. She tried to stand, but her knees buckled, and the city tilted beyond the glass. If the recording convinced them, the interview was only a trap. Footsteps approached in the hallway, heavy and deliberate, then stopped outside.

Rain striped the windows of the downtown office where Hannah waited for her job interview. She had rehearsed every answer while caring for her father through his final months, promising him she would apply when the position opened. Across the desk, the hiring manager skimmed her résumé, then closed the folder. “Your employment gap concerns us,” he said. Hannah explained the hospital visits, the medications, the nights spent beside a weakening hand. The manager glanced at the clock and thanked her for coming. In the elevator, her shoulders folded inward. She had expected questions about her skills, not a verdict on the time she had given away willingly. Outside, she reached for her phone to call her father, as she always did after difficult meetings. Her thumb hovered over his number before she remembered the silent room, the boxed clothes, the urn on the mantel. She sank onto a wet bench, pressed the phone to her chest, and wept while office workers streamed past.

Samuel arrived at the logistics office at 9:20 and entered a room with one table, three chairs, and two interviewers. After introductions, an interviewer placed twelve route cards beside four depot maps. Samuel divided 12 by 4 and stated that each map received 3 cards. The next prompt concerned warehouse capacity: 1,250 crates plus 375 crates equaled 1,625 crates. He wrote the total on a pad. For a staffing scenario, he subtracted 18 absent workers from 96 scheduled workers, producing 78 available workers. He then multiplied 14 vans by 8 parcels per van and obtained 112 parcels. “How would you check the schedule?” one interviewer asked. Samuel counted six morning rows and five afternoon rows, added 6 + 5 = 11, then compared that result with the eleven listed shifts. A final sheet showed 240 kilometers over 6 hours; he divided 240 by 6 to get 40 kilometers per hour. The interview lasted 45 minutes. Samuel returned the pencil, collected his coat, and left through the same door.

Hannah entered the office through a red door and checked in at a desk topped with crimson laminate. A receptionist wearing a burgundy scarf handed her a visitor card inside a scarlet sleeve. She sat beneath a muted red ceiling light, beside three chairs upholstered in ruby fabric. On the low table, a red ceramic bowl held pens with maroon caps. An interviewer arrived carrying a brick-red folder and led Hannah down a corridor striped with vermilion tiles. The meeting room contained a cherrywood table, two rust-colored chairs, and a carmine clock. “Please describe your previous role,” the interviewer said, opening the red folder. Hannah outlined her scheduling duties, spreadsheet work, and monthly reports while a ruby cursor moved across a wall display. She answered questions about deadlines and travel, then reviewed a salary range printed on rose-tinted paper. “We will contact you next week,” the interviewer said, returning the pages to the burgundy folder. Hannah collected her scarlet sleeve, crossed the red-tiled lobby, and departed through the crimson door.

Hannah arrived at the harbor office while the morning tide pressed seawater against the stone quay. Through the interview room windows, fishing boats crossed the bay, and gulls circled above the coastline. An interviewer beside a chart of shipping lanes asked Hannah about her previous work managing schedules for a coastal warehouse. She described tracking deliveries, checking invoices, and coordinating trucks with cargo vessels entering port on each tide. Beyond the glass, a ferry moved between green channel markers while harbor seals surfaced near its wake. “How would you handle a delayed shipment?” the interviewer asked as small waves folded along the seawall. Hannah explained that she would contact the crew, revise the dock schedule, and notify customers before the vessel reached the marina. A second interviewer took notes while a tugboat guided a freighter past the breakwater. The meeting ended when the tide began to recede, exposing bands of wet sand and scattered shells. Hannah left the harbor office and walked along the coast toward the bus stop.

Rain traced the windows of the sixth-floor conference room as Pavel sat before three interviewers. He had rehearsed every answer during the train ride, clutching the folder his father had helped him prepare. When the manager examined his résumé, he paused at the address and asked whether Pavel was related to the engineer who had worked there twenty years earlier. Pavel nodded. “He taught me everything I know.” The oldest interviewer lowered his pen and explained that Pavel’s father had designed the system the company still used, then added that they had planned to invite him back as a consultant. Pavel’s throat tightened. He had buried his father six days before and had applied for the job to fulfill their final promise. The interview continued, but the questions blurred beneath the hum of the lights. His hands shook under the table, and a drop struck the folder’s ink. When they offered him the position, he stared at the empty chair beside the door, wishing he could carry the news home.

Rain traced the office windows as Pavel sat across from three interviewers at a long oak table. He answered their questions carefully, describing how he had rescued a delayed project by reorganizing its schedule and helping two teams cooperate. When they presented a technical problem, he studied the diagram, spotted a hidden dependency, and proposed a solution on the whiteboard. The interviewers exchanged glances, then leaned forward with rapid follow-up questions. Pavel’s voice steadied as each answer connected neatly to the next. At last, the manager closed her notebook and said, “We would like to offer you the position.” For a second, Pavel remained perfectly still. Then warmth rushed through his chest, his face broke into a broad grin, and a laugh escaped him. He shook every offered hand, barely able to keep his feet planted. In the elevator, he read the written offer twice, pressed it to his chest, and silently pictured telling his family that all the late nights had worked.

Pavel sat across from three interviewers in a glass-walled conference room on the ninth floor. He answered each question carefully, outlining the projects he had led and the revenue they had produced. One interviewer glanced at his résumé, then asked whether he had actually managed the work or merely assisted. Pavel explained again, pointing to the figures beside his title. The interviewer smirked and slid the paper aside. “We need someone with real leadership experience.” Through the glass, Pavel saw a former colleague waiting outside, a man who had reported to him for two years. The panel welcomed that man warmly and praised credentials Pavel knew had been exaggerated. Heat climbed Pavel’s neck. His jaw locked until his teeth hurt, and his fingers crushed the leather folder in his lap. They had blocked him before he had entered, using his record as scrap while rewarding a polished lie. He stood so abruptly that the chair struck the wall. Without shaking hands, he took his résumé back and tore it once, slowly, before leaving the pieces on their table.

Pavel sat beneath fluorescent lights in a glass-walled conference room on the thirty-second floor. Across the table, two interviewers turned pages in his résumé while a third studied a laptop. The questions began routinely, and Pavel described projects, deadlines, and the years he had spent at his previous company. Then the laptop user rotated the screen. A security photograph showed Pavel leaving that company’s records office after midnight, carrying the folder he had anonymously delivered to investigators. “Can you explain this?” the interviewer asked. Pavel’s mouth dried. His pulse hammered against his collar, and sweat slid between his shoulder blades. He glanced toward the door; one interviewer quietly locked it. They knew. Perhaps his former employer had sent them, and perhaps this interview had never concerned a job. His chair scraped as he stood, but his knees buckled against the table. Beyond the glass, two uniformed guards approached. Pavel searched for another exit and found only sealed windows, far above the street.

Pavel arrived at the office building shortly before his scheduled job interview. He checked the directory in the lobby, took the elevator, and reported his name at the reception desk. A receptionist asked him to sign a visitor sheet and directed him to a row of chairs. Pavel sat, placed his document folder on his lap, and watched employees pass through a glass door. After several minutes, an interviewer called his name and led him into a meeting room. “Please have a seat,” the interviewer said. Pavel sat across from the desk and handed over a copy of his résumé. The interviewer asked about his previous duties, his software experience, and his availability. Pavel answered each question in a steady voice and gave brief examples from his last workplace. He then asked about the daily schedule and reporting structure. The interviewer described the position, noted the next stage of the hiring process, and collected his papers. Pavel thanked the interviewer, returned his visitor badge, and left the building.

Pavel arrived for the job interview at an office overlooking the harbor, where fishing boats moved between stone piers. Seawater tapped the pilings below as a receptionist directed him to a room with broad windows facing the coastline. Across the bay, gulls circled above a cargo ship, and silver fish turned near the surface. The interviewer entered carrying a folder marked with the emblem of a marine survey company. Waves crossed the outer channel while Pavel described his experience maintaining navigation records and scheduling crews. “How would you organize work around the tides?” the interviewer asked. Pavel explained that he would compare tide tables, vessel timetables, and dock availability before assigning tasks. A ferry passed beyond the glass, leaving a white wake that spread toward anchored sailboats. The interviewer asked about equipment inventories, and Pavel outlined a system for cataloging sonar units, ropes, buoys, and sample containers. Outside, the tide exposed bands of dark seaweed along the quay. After several notes were added to the folder, Pavel received a date for the hiring decision and departed beside the calm harbor.

Pavel arrived for a job interview at a warehouse planning office and took the chair opposite two managers. One manager described daily shipments, while the other recorded his answers. Pavel calculated that 24 morning deliveries plus 18 afternoon deliveries equaled 42 total deliveries. For inventory, he subtracted 37 dispatched crates from 96 stored crates: 96 - 37 = 59 crates remaining. Asked about packing capacity, he multiplied 14 pallets by 6 boxes per pallet and stated that 14 × 6 = 84 boxes. He then divided 144 labels among 12 workers: 144 ÷ 12 = 12 labels each. A manager added a scheduling question. Pavel combined 35 regular orders with 15 special orders, obtaining 35 + 15 = 50, then divided 50 orders across 5 loading bays to get 10 orders per bay. He checked a final stock adjustment: 80 - 26 = 54 units. The managers reviewed their notes, explained the position’s routine, and ended the interview after 32 minutes. Pavel collected his folder and left the office.

At dusk, every house on Fatima’s street went dark while the avenue beyond remained brightly lit. She found the utility crew beside an open transformer box and learned that service had been restored to the newer development first. An official waved her away, saying her neighborhood would have to wait until morning. “We reported the broken lines yesterday,” Fatima said. He shrugged and climbed into his truck. Heat surged up her neck. She watched the truck roll toward streets where porch lamps already glowed, and her jaw tightened until her teeth ached. Her freezer held medicine for an elderly neighbor, yet their calls had been ignored while wealthier blocks received immediate repairs. Fatima slammed her palm against the utility pole, then snatched up her phone. She photographed the departing crew, the darkened homes, and the illuminated development beyond. “They will answer for this,” she said. She began knocking on doors, gathering residents and evidence, each step sharpening the hot pressure behind her ribs.

Fatima was rinsing a cup when the kitchen light went out. The refrigerator stopped humming, and the clock above the stove showed a blank screen. She closed the tap, dried the cup, and placed it in the cupboard. From the hallway, a neighbor opened a door and asked whether the power was out in every apartment. Fatima checked the landing and saw that the ceiling lamps were off. Outside, several windows along the street were dark. A shopkeeper stood near the entrance of a small grocery, holding a flashlight over the counter. Fatima returned inside and found a candle in a drawer. She set it in a jar, lit it, and continued sorting the mail on the table. A bus passed at the corner, and its headlights moved across the wall. After a while, the refrigerator started again. The clock blinked, and the hallway lamps came on. Fatima blew out the candle, opened a window, and washed the jar.

Fatima lived beside a harbor where the tide marked the seawall twice each day. At dusk, the neighborhood power failed while fishing boats crossed the darkening bay. Streetlamps along the coastline went out, and apartment windows reflected only seawater and the pale wakes of ferries. Fatima placed a battery lantern on her table beside a jar of shells. From the balcony, she watched neighbors gather near the marina, where ropes tapped against masts and small waves folded under the docks. “The current is off,” someone said, pointing inland from the harbor. Fatima checked her refrigerator, then closed it while gulls moved above the tidal flats. Shopkeepers near the fish market set candles beside baskets painted with octopuses and sardines. Children counted cargo ships beyond the breakwater as adults consulted their phones. After an hour, lights returned along the coast in a sequence like buoys. Fatima switched off the lantern, opened the curtains toward the bay, and recorded the outage beside the morning’s tide times.

At dusk, every window on Fatima’s street went black, and the streetlamps vanished with them. Neighbors stepped onto porches holding candles and phones, while children traced flashlight beams across the pavement. Fatima stayed inside beside an old answering machine connected to a backup battery. Once each week, she played the final message her mother had left before dying, a brief reminder to water the basil and wear a scarf. The battery light flickered. When the electricity returned, a sharp surge snapped through the room, and the machine gave a thin click. Fatima pressed the message button. Nothing played. She pressed it again, then unplugged the machine and held it against her ear as if a voice might remain inside. “Please,” she whispered. Outside, houses brightened one by one, and neighbors applauded. Fatima sank to the kitchen floor. Her throat tightened until swallowing hurt, and tears spotted the machine’s dusty buttons. The basil stood dry on the sill, its leaves curled inward.

At nine o’clock, every house on Fatima’s street went dark, and the electric fans slowed to silence. She found a candle in the kitchen drawer and lit it, watching shadows climb the walls. Outside, neighbors gathered with phone lights, but Fatima stayed beside her sleeping daughter. Then the back gate scraped open. She froze. The gate had been bolted before sunset. Footsteps crossed the yard, slow and heavy, crushing the dry leaves beneath the window. Her breath snagged, and hot blood pounded in her ears. She locked the kitchen door, lifted her daughter from bed, and crouched with her inside the wardrobe. “Stay quiet,” she whispered. The footsteps reached the porch. A hand tested the door, then shoved hard enough to rattle the frame. Fatima clamped both hands over her mouth to smother a cry. She pictured the bolt splitting, the dark figure entering. Suddenly, porch lights flared across the street. Someone ran from the yard, and neighbors began shouting. Fatima remained hidden, trembling long after the electricity returned.

At 8:12 p.m., the neighborhood power went out, and Fatima placed three battery lamps on the kitchen table. She counted 24 apartments across four buildings and calculated 24 ÷ 4 = 6 apartments per building. Each lamp held two batteries, so 3 × 2 = 6 batteries were in use. A drawer contained 11 spare batteries; after she gave 4 to neighbors, 11 − 4 = 7 remained. Outside, residents gathered near the entrance while someone checked the electrical panel. Fatima noted that 9 candles from one household plus 8 from another made 9 + 8 = 17 candles. She divided them among 17 doorways, calculating 17 ÷ 17 = 1 candle per doorway. The outage lasted from 8:12 to 9:03, which she recorded as 48 + 3 = 51 minutes. When the lights returned, she measured the remaining lamp time: 120 − 51 = 69 minutes. She collected two lamps, left one with an upstairs resident, and wrote that 3 − 1 = 2 lamps came home.

At dusk, every house on Malik’s block went dark, and the streetlights blinked out. He found candles in a kitchen drawer, then carried a flashlight onto the porch. Neighbors emerged with lanterns, folding chairs, and food that would spoil without refrigeration. Malik helped arrange a shared table beneath the maple trees. Someone brought a guitar, children traced circles with glow sticks, and an elderly neighbor passed around melting ice cream. Then Malik remembered the telescope packed in his closet. He set it on the sidewalk and aimed it above the black rooftops, where the powerless neighborhood left the sky startlingly clear. Through the lens, Saturn floated like a golden bead with delicate rings. “Come look,” Malik said. One by one, the neighbors bent to the eyepiece and gasped. Malik’s grin stretched until his cheeks ached. Warmth rushed through his chest, and he bounced on his heels, laughing as the whole block gathered around his telescope. For once, everything had gone perfectly right in the dark.

When the neighborhood lost power, Fatima set a red flashlight on the crimson tablecloth beside the window. Across the street, dark houses held faint reflections from red curtains, burgundy shutters, and a parked scarlet bicycle. She opened a red metal cabinet and counted three ruby-colored candles, though she left them unlit. In the hallway, neighbors carried maroon cushions and vermilion thermos flasks toward the shared courtyard. Fatima brought a red wool blanket, a brick-red radio, and a bowl painted with carmine stripes. “The batteries still work,” she said, turning the red dial until a local station became clear. Under the deep red evening sky, the group listened while someone distributed cups of hibiscus tea on a cherry-colored tray. A child rolled a crimson ball between two red garden pots, and an older resident arranged coral playing cards on a burgundy mat. When the electricity returned, red lampshades glowed along the windows, and Fatima folded her scarlet blanket before carrying the ruby candles back inside.

Hannah arrived at the office at 9:20 and signed the visitor log. Before the interview, she reviewed a sample staffing table: 14 morning workers plus 9 afternoon workers equaled 23 workers. In the conference room, two interviewers asked how she would organize a shipment. Hannah wrote, “Six pallets times 24 boxes equals 144 boxes.” She then divided 144 boxes by 8 shelves and obtained 18 boxes per shelf. For an inventory adjustment, she subtracted 37 duplicate labels from 215 labels, leaving 178 usable labels. Another prompt concerned weekly reports. Five departments producing 12 reports each made 5 × 12 = 60 reports, and adding 7 revised reports gave 67. She also calculated that a four-hour task split among two workers required 4 ÷ 2 = 2 hours per worker. One interviewer described the position’s rotating schedule and recordkeeping procedures. Hannah asked about training, entered two notes in her folder, and returned the pen. The meeting lasted 45 minutes, from 9:30 to 10:15. She signed out and took the elevator downstairs.

Pavel arrived at the office wearing a red tie beneath a charcoal coat, and he wiped a trace of red dust from his shoes. The receptionist handed him a crimson badge and directed him past red chairs, ruby planters, and a maroon carpet. In the interview room, red blinds divided the gray daylight into narrow scarlet bands across the table. Two interviewers sat beside vermilion folders, while Pavel placed his résumé near a red ceramic pencil cup. “Describe your previous position,” one interviewer said, turning a burgundy page. Pavel outlined his duties, his schedule, and the reports he had prepared under a department logo printed in dark red. He then answered questions about spreadsheets, deadlines, and travel as a red clock moved above shelves lined with russet binders. One interviewer recorded notes with a scarlet pen; the other adjusted a red linen cuff and listed the role’s tasks. At the end, Pavel received a maroon envelope containing the timetable for the next stage, then crossed the red-tiled lobby and left.

At nine o’clock, every window on Fatima’s street went black beneath a sky crowded with stars. She found candles, then carried a lantern to the apartment courtyard, where neighbors were gathering with thawing food and folding chairs. Someone produced a grill, and soon pans hissed while children traced circles of light across the walls. Fatima fetched her old oud, though she had not played before others in years. Her fingers stumbled during the first tune, then settled into the rhythm. One by one, voices joined her. “Keep going,” an elderly neighbor said. Fatima began a faster song her mother had taught her. The courtyard clapped in perfect time. A little girl spun between the chairs, and even people on balconies sang the chorus. Warmth surged through Fatima’s chest; her grin widened until her cheeks ached, and laughter spilled out between verses. When the streetlights suddenly blinked on, nobody moved indoors. Fatima lifted the oud again, marveling that her song had united the block, and played louder as everyone cheered.

At nine o’clock, every house on Malik’s block went dark, and the streetlights vanished with them. He found a flashlight in the kitchen drawer and stepped onto the porch, where neighbors clustered with candles and phones. Across the road, a transformer crackled blue, then fell silent. Malik was turning back inside when slow footsteps scraped along the narrow passage beside his house. His flashlight beam shook across the fence and caught a hand withdrawing through an open basement window. Someone was inside. His throat tightened, and cold sweat gathered under his collar. He backed away, fumbling for his phone, but the screen showed no signal. From below came the thud of a door, followed by careful steps climbing the basement stairs. “Who’s there?” he called. No answer came. Malik’s pulse hammered against his ribs. He pictured the unlocked kitchen, the dark hallway, the approaching intruder. When the back doorknob began to turn, he sprinted toward the neighbors, barely able to breathe.

Malik was rinsing a plate when the kitchen light went out and the refrigerator stopped humming. He set the plate in the rack, dried his hands, and looked through the window. The neighboring houses were dark, and someone across the street opened a front door. Malik found a flashlight in a drawer and placed it on the counter. He checked the breaker panel, but its switches remained in place. In the hallway, a neighbor said the whole block had lost power. Malik nodded and returned inside. He unplugged the television and the toaster, then closed the refrigerator door firmly. With the flashlight beside him, he sat at the table and sorted a stack of mail. Outside, several people stood near their gates while a utility truck moved slowly along the road. After a while, the streetlights came on. The refrigerator resumed humming, and the microwave clock blinked. Malik plugged in the toaster, put away the mail, and finished washing the plate.

At dusk, every house on Malik’s block went dark, and the streetlights vanished with them. He found a flashlight and stepped outside, where neighbors gathered beside stalled porch fans and silent radios. From the house next door came the thin beeping of a battery alarm. Malik remembered the older woman’s oxygen machine and hurried across her yard. He knocked, called through the screen, then tried the unlocked door. “Can you hear me?” he asked. The machine stood beside her chair, its tubes still looped beneath her nose, but its display was black. Malik pressed two fingers to her wrist and found nothing. He called for help, though his voice broke so badly he had to repeat the address. When the paramedics covered her face, his knees struck the carpet. He stared at the powerless outlet, remembering how she had brought him soup each winter. Outside, the lights returned window by window. Malik remained on the floor, shaking, one hand clenched around the useless plug.

At nine o’clock, every house on Malik’s block went dark beneath a windless summer sky. He found candles for his grandmother, then stepped outside and saw porch lights glowing across the avenue. A utility truck idled at the corner, where a crew had restored power to the newer development but left his row unconnected. Malik approached the supervisor and explained that medical equipment in several homes required electricity. The supervisor barely looked up. “Your section can wait until morning.” Moments later, another worker admitted they had the necessary fuse, but the supervisor ordered the truck away because the residents’ repeated complaints had been rude. Heat climbed Malik’s neck. His jaw locked until his teeth hurt, and his hands curled around the outage notice. They paid the same rates; why were they being punished for demanding service? He planted himself before the truck, photographed its number, and called the emergency utility line. When the supervisor threatened police, Malik did not move. Behind him, neighbors raised their phones, and the crew finally opened the repair box.

When the neighborhood lost power, Malik stood beside a red curtain and watched the lamps along the street go dark. He took a red flashlight from a crimson drawer and aimed its narrow red beam across the kitchen tiles. Outside, neighbors gathered near a maroon gate, carrying scarlet lanterns, ruby-colored torches, and red plastic stools. Malik crossed the porch in burgundy slippers and placed a red folding chair beside the steps. A child rolled a vermilion ball along the pavement while two adults checked a red utility box without opening it. The sunset left a copper-red strip above the roofs, and dark red clouds moved over the silent wires. Malik used a brick-red radio with fresh batteries to hear a report about the outage. Several windows displayed red blankets, red vases, or rust-colored blinds in the remaining daylight. After an hour, the streetlights returned, casting pale light onto the red benches. Malik switched off his crimson flashlight, folded the red chair, and went indoors.

At 7:12 p.m., the power went out across Agnes’s neighborhood. She placed four candles on the kitchen table and counted her supplies. Three drawers held 6 candles each, so 3 × 6 = 18 candles. After using 4, she had 18 − 4 = 14. She divided them between 2 rooms: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 per room. Outside, 9 houses on one side of the street and 11 on the other were dark, making 9 + 11 = 20 houses. Agnes checked two battery packs. Each contained 8 batteries, so 2 × 8 = 16 batteries; 5 were already used, leaving 16 − 5 = 11. A neighbor knocked and reported that repair crews expected service within 90 minutes. Agnes used 30 minutes to prepare food and 20 to arrange flashlights, totaling 30 + 20 = 50 minutes. That left 90 − 50 = 40 minutes. At 8:42, the lamps switched on, and she stored the remaining candles.

Agnes was rinsing a plate when the kitchen light went out. The refrigerator stopped humming, and the clock above the stove lost its display. She turned off the tap, dried her hands, and looked through the window. Several houses across the street were also dark. A neighbor stepped onto a porch and checked the nearby lamps. Agnes opened a drawer, found a flashlight, and set it on the counter. She unplugged the kettle and the television, then placed the unfinished plate beside the sink. Outside, a utility truck moved slowly along the road and stopped near the corner. Two workers examined a box beside a pole. Agnes sat at the table and sorted the mail by the flashlight. After a while, the refrigerator started again, the clock display returned, and lights appeared in the neighboring windows. She reset the clock, plugged in the kettle, finished washing the plate, and closed the curtains. The truck left before she made tea.

When the neighborhood power failed, Agnes set a red enamel lantern on the kitchen table. Its crimson shade remained dark, so she opened the scarlet curtains and watched burgundy rooftops under the evening sky. Across the street, residents placed red candles, unlit, in ruby glass holders beside their windows. Agnes carried a vermilion cushion to the porch and sat near a rust-colored railing. A neighbor in a maroon sweater checked the silent meter boxes, while another arranged red paper cups on a brick-red tray. “The utility crew is coming,” someone said beneath a cherry-colored umbrella. Agnes noted the time with a red pencil on a sheet of rose stationery. Along the pavement, parked cars reflected the dim garnet sunset, and crimson bicycles leaned against terracotta walls. After an hour, the streetlamps returned, casting pale red light through their tinted covers. Appliances resumed behind red doors and coppery blinds. Agnes closed the scarlet curtains, returned the red cushion, and placed the ruby holder in a cupboard.

At dusk, every house on Agnes’s street went dark except the new apartments at the corner. She found the utility crew beside a humming generator and asked when power would return. A worker checked his clipboard and said, “Your block is scheduled for tomorrow.” Agnes pointed to the bright apartments, where hallway lamps glowed and televisions flickered behind windows. The worker admitted their manager had paid for priority service, then turned away to coil a cable. Heat climbed Agnes’s neck. Her groceries were spoiling, her oxygen-dependent neighbor sat trapped upstairs, and money had apparently purchased a place ahead of them. She gripped the barricade until its metal edge cut her palm. “You skipped us because they paid.” The worker shrugged. Something hard and scorching spread through her chest. Agnes photographed the clipboard, the generator, and the illuminated building, then called every local reporter whose number she could find. When the crew tried to move the barricade, she planted herself before it, jaw locked, refusing to let their quiet injustice remain hidden.

At dusk, every house on Agnes’s street went dark, and the traffic lights blinked out. She found candles, then carried a lantern onto the porch, where neighbors were gathering with flashlights and blankets. From across the road came the thin wail of a child whose birthday cake had not finished baking. Agnes remembered the camping oven in her shed. She hauled it out, checked the fuel, and set the half-baked cake inside while everyone watched the little thermometer rise. Minutes later, a warm vanilla scent drifted down the sidewalk. When she lifted the lid, the cake stood golden and firm. The child clapped, and neighbors began tapping spoons against mugs. “You saved it,” someone said. Agnes’s breath caught. A laugh burst from her and kept spilling out as candles were pressed into the frosting. Her cheeks ached from grinning. When the whole street sang beneath the powerless windows, she thought the blackout had somehow switched on everything that mattered.

Agnes lived beside a harbor where fishing boats shifted with the evening tide. When the neighborhood power failed, the shoreline houses became dark shapes above the seawall. Agnes placed a lamp on her table, though its glass reflected only moonlight from the bay. Outside, several residents gathered near the marina, where ropes tapped masts and small waves folded against the docks. “The harbor office is checking the lines,” someone said. Agnes walked along the coastal road while gulls crossed above the water and seals surfaced beyond the moored vessels. Shopkeepers set lanterns beside baskets of shellfish, and diners continued eating near windows facing the black sea. The lighthouse remained active on its separate circuit, sending measured bands across the channel. Agnes reached the pier and watched a ferry approach from the outer coastline, its deck lights mirrored in the tide. After an hour, electricity returned along the waterfront, and windows brightened between the harbor and the beach. Agnes went home as the waves continued their regular passage over the sand.

At dusk, every house on Agnes’s block went dark, and the streetlamps vanished with them. She lit two candles and carried one to the hallway table, where an old answering machine waited beneath a film of dust. For three years, she had guarded the final message her mother had left before the hospital called. During storms, Agnes sometimes pressed play just to hear that thin voice say, “I’ll ring tomorrow.” The electricity returned with a violent flicker. The machine clicked, whined, and released a thread of smoke. Agnes unplugged it, then pressed every button, slowly at first, then hard enough to whiten her knuckles. The tape would not turn. She opened the casing and found the ribbon curled and blackened around the spindle. Her breath hitched. She lowered herself onto the floor, clutching the ruined tape against her chest. Outside, windows shone again, televisions resumed, and neighbors cheered. Agnes rocked beside the table until the candle drowned in its own wax.

At dusk beside the harbor, Malik noticed that every house along the coastline had gone dark while the tide slid past the seawall. He checked his apartment’s breaker, then looked through the window at fishing boats resting on level seawater without their dock lights. Along the street, neighbors carried battery lanterns between buildings painted with shells, gulls, and blue waves. “The whole neighborhood is out,” someone said near a shop that sold nets and preserved seaweed. Malik placed a lamp on his balcony, where its pale circle touched a railing crusted with salt from the bay. He ate bread and tinned sardines while the harbor buoys blinked on their own batteries beyond the darkened pier. After an hour, utility workers arrived by the coastal road and opened a cabinet beside a mural of whales. Malik watched a ferry cross the moonlit channel as power returned in sections, first to the marina office and then to the apartments. Refrigerators resumed humming above the sound of small waves, and Malik reset his stove clock before the tide turned.

At dusk, every house on Dmitri’s street went dark, and the streetlamps vanished beneath a cloudy sky. He found candles, checked the fuse box, then carried a flashlight outside. Neighbors stood on porches while rainwater streamed along the curb. Across the road, an elderly resident’s oxygen machine had stopped, and its backup battery was nearly empty. Dmitri remembered the small generator buried in his garage. He dragged it through the rain, fumbled with the fuel valve, and pulled the starter cord until his shoulders burned. The engine coughed once, twice, then settled into a steady roar. A lamp glowed behind the resident’s window, and the oxygen machine began humming. “It’s working,” someone called. Dmitri threw both arms overhead. A laugh burst from him, loud enough to rise above the engine, and his chest seemed too full for a single breath. Neighbors clapped and hurried over with extension cords. As refrigerators and medical devices flickered back to life, Dmitri grinned until his cheeks ached.

Malik was stacking dishes when the neighborhood lights went out at 7:18. He counted twelve windows across the street and found that five still showed battery lanterns: 12 - 5 = 7 windows were dark. In a kitchen drawer, he located four flashlights, each holding two cells, so 4 × 2 = 8 cells were installed. He checked a box containing fourteen spare cells and divided them among seven neighbors: 14 ÷ 7 = 2 cells per neighbor. The building’s hallway had three floors with six doors on each, making 3 × 6 = 18 doors to visit. After nine doors received candles, 18 - 9 = 9 remained. Malik set two candles on each of those nine mats, calculating 9 × 2 = 18 candles. The outage lasted from 7:18 until 8:06, or 48 minutes, because 66 - 18 = 48. He added two power-bank capacities, 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000 milliamp-hours, then assigned 10,000 ÷ 5 = 2,000 to each of five phones. When the streetlights returned, he resumed stacking dishes.

At dusk, every house on Dmitri’s street went dark except the new apartment tower at the corner. Dmitri found the utility crew beside an open transformer box and asked when service would return. A supervisor glanced at his address, then waved him back. “Your block can wait until morning.” Behind the barricade, workers connected a portable generator to the tower while its lobby lights blazed and its rooftop sign shimmered. Dmitri had reported the failing transformer three times, but the company had closed each complaint without inspection. Now groceries spoiled in his refrigerator, his medical equipment sat useless, and paying tenants in the tower received priority. Heat climbed his neck. He gripped the barricade until the metal rattled, imagining the supervisor’s clipboard snapping between his hands. When a worker ordered him away, Dmitri planted his boots on the asphalt. “You ignored us for months.” His jaw throbbed from clenching it. He began calling every darkened house, gathering neighbors and complaint numbers, determined that no truck would leave quietly.

At nine o’clock, every house on Dmitri’s street went dark. He found a candle in the kitchen drawer and carried it to the window, where neighbors stood on porches holding flashlights. The power lines hung motionless above the road. Then a transformer box at the corner burst with a blue flash, and something heavy scraped along the side of his house. Dmitri froze. Three slow knocks sounded from the basement door beneath his feet. His throat tightened, and the candle shook in his hand, spilling wax across his knuckles. He told himself a fallen branch had struck the wall, but the knocks came again, louder and closer together. “Who’s there?” he called. No one answered. The basement latch began to lift. Dmitri backed toward the front door, unable to draw a full breath, while blackness seemed to press into every room. When the latch clicked open, he ran outside barefoot and did not stop until he reached the crowded porch across the street.

At nine, every house on Agnes’s block went dark, and the streetlamps blinked out together. She found a candle, lit it, and carried it toward the kitchen, where rain tapped the windows. Outside, neighbors moved between porches with flashlights. Then someone shouted about a gas smell. Agnes reached for her phone, but it had no signal. A dull thud sounded beneath the floorboards. Another followed, directly under her feet. The candle flame trembled as she backed away. “Is anyone there?” she called. Metal scraped below, then the basement door handle slowly turned. Agnes’s throat tightened. She remembered locking that door after bringing up laundry. The handle stopped, then jerked harder. Her pulse hammered against her ribs, and sweat chilled her neck. She snatched a heavy pan and stumbled toward the front entrance, imagining flames racing through the pipes or a stranger climbing the stairs. Behind her, the basement latch clicked open. Agnes ran into the rain without looking back.

At dusk, every house on Dmitri’s street went dark, and the traffic lights beyond the rooftops blinked out. He found a candle, then hurried to the living room where his father’s old aquarium stood silent. The filter had stopped, and the heater’s red coil was black. Inside, the last fish his father had bred drifted near the gravel, its silver gills working too quickly. Dmitri wrapped the tank in blankets and tried pouring water between two cups to give it air. “Stay with me,” he whispered. Hours passed without the power returning. Just before dawn, the fish rolled onto its side. Dmitri dipped both hands into the cold water and lifted it, though he knew there was nothing to save. Its scales gleamed in the candlelight like the cuff links buried with his father. His chest folded inward. He sat on the wet carpet, holding the tiny body until his fingers cramped, and understood that the last living thing they had tended together was gone.

At dusk, Dmitri was rinsing a cup when the kitchen light went out. The refrigerator stopped humming, and the clock above the stove showed a blank screen. He turned the tap off, dried his hands, and looked through the window. Several apartments across the courtyard were also dark. In the hallway, a neighbor opened a door and said, “The whole block is out.” Dmitri returned to the kitchen and found a flashlight in a drawer. He set it on the table, then unplugged the kettle and computer. Outside, a few residents stood near the entrance while a utility van moved slowly along the street. Dmitri carried a chair to the balcony and watched vehicles pass through the intersection under the direction of a worker. After a while, he went inside, sliced bread, and ate it with cheese. The lights came on as he washed the plate. He reset the stove clock, plugged in the kettle, and closed the curtains.

When the neighborhood lost power, Dmitri stood beside a red-curtained window and watched the brick buildings fade into a deep maroon dusk. He took a red flashlight from a crimson drawer, but left it switched off while the remaining daylight crossed the scarlet rug. In the hallway, neighbors carried red candles without lighting them, and one person held a ruby-colored battery lantern. “The whole block is out,” someone said beside a burgundy door. Dmitri descended the stairs, passing red mailboxes, rust-red pipes, and a vermilion bicycle chained beneath the awning. Outside, residents gathered near a red bench while the unlit shops displayed carmine signs and folded crimson umbrellas. Dmitri checked the utility box, whose dull red paint matched the clay paving stones, then wrote the outage time in a small cardinal-red notebook. When the electricity returned, red lampshades glowed through several windows, the ruby lantern was packed away, and Dmitri went upstairs beneath the maroon evening sky.

Dmitri was rinsing salt from a bucket when the harbor neighborhood lost power. Across the seawall, apartment windows darkened one by one above the tide. The fish market closed its electric shutters halfway, leaving rows of mackerel visible beside trays of ice. Dmitri set the bucket near a coil of rope and checked the coastal circuit panel. Along the pier, shopkeepers placed battery lanterns among nets, shells, and jars of seawater. “The whole district is out,” a neighbor said while gulls crossed above the anchored boats. Dmitri noted the time as a ferry moved through the channel beyond the breakwater. Without refrigeration, vendors covered squid and sea bass with additional ice from insulated boxes. The tide reached the lower harbor steps while electricians inspected cables beneath the waterfront street. After forty minutes, lamps returned across the marina, reflecting in narrow bands on the water. Dmitri switched off the lantern, finished rinsing the bucket, and watched a cargo ship follow the coastline toward the open sea.

Morning sunlight fell across the raised beds of the neighborhood community garden. Mei knelt beside the tomato patch, guiding a wilted vine around its stake. For weeks, she and the other gardeners had hauled compost, repaired irrigation lines, and watched tiny blossoms drop before fruit formed. That morning, she parted the leaves and discovered a cluster of red tomatoes, round and unblemished. Nearby, beans coiled over their trellis, squash crowded the mulch, and bees moved among the marigolds. “Come look,” she called. Neighbors gathered, pointing as they found peppers, cucumbers, and strawberries tucked beneath green leaves. A laugh burst from Mei before she could stop it. She sprang up, clapped both soil-streaked hands, and spun once between the beds. Her chest felt almost too full for breathing. The garden had worked; their patience had become baskets of food. As everyone began picking, Mei grinned until her cheeks ached and carried the first overflowing basket toward the shared table.

The community garden stretched between two apartment blocks, its narrow beds divided by brick paths and wire trellises. Mei arrived before sunrise carrying tomato seedlings and found yellow notices stapled to the gate. The city had sold the land, and demolition would begin Monday. She read the notice twice, then pressed one palm against the damp wood. Around her, neighbors gathered in slippers and work clothes, speaking in low, broken phrases. “They cannot take this,” someone said. Mei stepped inside and walked to the peach tree her mother had planted twelve years earlier. Its first blossoms trembled above the bench where they had once shelled peas together. She sank onto the wet soil, heedless of the mud soaking her knees. Her throat closed when she pictured bulldozers crushing the roots, the painted stones, the crooked sign in her mother’s handwriting. She tried to dig up the tree, but each root she cut felt like another farewell. At last, the shovel slipped from her hands, and she folded over the trunk, weeping until noon.

Morning light fell across the raised beds of the neighborhood community garden. Mei arrived carrying tomato seedlings she had nurtured for six weeks, only to find her assigned plot stripped bare. A committee member explained that another gardener had claimed it after Mei missed one Saturday meeting, though the posted rules allowed three absences. Her seedlings trembled in their paper pots as her grip tightened. “That rule applies to everyone,” Mei said. The member shrugged and pointed toward a narrow patch beside the dumpsters, where the soil glittered with broken glass. Heat rushed up Mei’s neck. She pictured the hours spent turning compost, repairing fences, and hauling water for plots that were not hers. Now they expected her to accept scraps without protest. She set the seedlings down before she crushed them, marched to the notice board, and tore off the false assignment sheet. Then she photographed the rules, the ruined plot, and every committee signature. Her jaw ached from clenching. She would call a full meeting, and no shrug would stop her.

Mei worked in a community garden beside the harbor, where seawater tapped the stone wall at each rising tide. She measured plots while fishing boats crossed the bay and gulls circled above the coastline. Salt wind moved through rows of chard, and oyster shells lined the paths between shared beds. Mei mixed seaweed compost into the soil as waves folded across the nearby beach. Other gardeners planted beans, squash, and coastal herbs while a ferry passed beyond the breakwater. At noon, Mei checked a rain barrel decorated with painted crabs and filled watering cans beside a rack of drying nets. “The tide turns at two,” someone said near the tool shed. Mei recorded the time, then trimmed kale leaves marked by salt spray. In the afternoon, harbor water reflected sails while neighbors divided tomatoes and inspected the kelp mulch. Mei closed the garden gate after the tide began to recede, and small shorebirds searched the wet coastline beyond the plots.

Morning sunlight striped the raised beds of the community garden, where tomatoes climbed twine beside rows of beans. Mei knelt near the tool shed, pressing seedlings into damp soil while two neighbors carried mulch along the path. A sharp crack split the air. The shed’s roof lurched, and a heavy branch crashed through it, scattering shingles across the bed where a child had been watering moments earlier. Another branch groaned overhead. Mei froze, dirt clutched between her fingers. The trunk of the old maple had opened in a jagged seam, and the whole crown leaned toward the gardeners. Her pulse hammered against her throat. “Get to the gate,” she said, but her voice barely emerged. Wind stirred the leaves, and the split widened with a splintering pop. Mei seized the child’s wrist and ran, expecting the shadow above them to drop. Her knees shook so badly she stumbled at the gate. Behind them, the maple tilted another inch, creaking as everyone crowded onto the pavement.

Morning sunlight lay across the raised beds of the neighborhood garden, glinting on wet leaves and wire trellises. Omar unlocked the gate and carried two watering cans toward the tomato patch. For weeks, the plants had drooped despite compost, careful pruning, and daily visits from volunteers. He knelt beside the tallest vine, parted its curled leaves, and stopped. Beneath them hung three round tomatoes, deep red and unblemished. Farther down the row, more crimson fruit clustered under nearly every branch. “They made it,” he whispered. His breath caught, then burst out as laughter. He sprang up so quickly that water sloshed over his shoes. Clapping his muddy hands, he waved the arriving gardeners toward the beds. Soon baskets filled, children counted tomatoes, and neighbors passed slices around on a wooden board. Omar tasted one, warm from the sun, and grinned until his cheeks ached. The garden buzzed around him, and he thought of all those patient mornings. He lifted a brimming basket above his head and laughed again.

Mei arrived at the community garden after breakfast and unlatched the narrow gate. She placed her canvas bag beside the tool shed, chose a hand fork, and walked to her assigned bed. The soil around the bean plants had formed a light crust, so she loosened it in short rows and pulled several small weeds. She dropped the weeds into a bucket for the compost pile. At the next bed, a neighbor tied tomato stems to wooden stakes while another person filled watering cans at the tap. Mei carried one can along the path and poured water near the roots of her beans and lettuce. A sparrow landed on the fence, pecked at a post, and flew toward the roofs. After watering, Mei checked the undersides of several leaves and removed a damaged one. She swept loose soil from the path, returned the fork to the shed, and emptied her bucket into the compost bin. Before leaving, she closed the gate and wiped her shoes on the mat.

Mei entered the community garden at eight and counted 6 raised beds, each holding 12 lettuce plants, so 6 × 12 = 72 plants. She checked the watering chart: 48 liters divided among 6 beds gave 48 ÷ 6 = 8 liters per bed. Along the eastern fence, 27 bean seedlings stood in one row and 15 in another; 27 + 15 = 42 seedlings. She removed 9 cracked labels from a box of 34, leaving 34 − 9 = 25 usable labels. Two neighbors carried compost while Mei measured paths. Three paths were 7 meters long, making 3 × 7 = 21 meters, and a fourth added 5 meters, for 21 + 5 = 26 meters. “Eight liters here,” she said. At noon, 18 radishes were split into 3 baskets, so 18 ÷ 3 = 6 per basket. Mei recorded 72 + 42 = 114 growing plants, then subtracted 11 empty spaces: 114 − 11 = 103 occupied spots. She closed the shed after counting 4 rakes, 2 hoes, and 1 spade, totaling 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 tools.

Morning sunlight striped the raised beds of the community garden, where Omar watered tomatoes beside the tool shed. As he dragged the hose toward the beans, a sharp hissing rose behind him. He turned and saw smoke curling from the shed’s cracked window. Then came a thud from inside, followed by a child’s muffled cough. Omar dropped the nozzle. His heart slammed against his ribs, and his hands shook so badly that the latch slipped twice beneath his fingers. Flames flickered along a shelf stacked with fertilizer and fuel cans. The sight hollowed his stomach. Any second, he thought, the cans could burst. “Stay low,” he called. He wrapped his sleeve over his mouth and crawled through the doorway, each pop from the burning wood tightening his chest. He found the child beneath a fallen rake rack, pulled the boards aside, and dragged them both into the path. Behind them, a can ruptured with a metallic crack. Omar kept running until his knees buckled among the cabbages.

Morning sunlight fell across the raised beds of the community garden, where tomatoes climbed wire cages beside rows of beans. Omar arrived carrying seedlings he had nurtured for weeks, but stopped when he saw his assigned plot stripped bare. A new wooden sign claimed it for another gardener. The coordinator explained that the committee had reassigned his bed after someone reported he had abandoned it, though Omar had watered it every evening. “There was a vote,” the coordinator said. No one had told him about any meeting. Heat surged into his face, and his grip crushed the cardboard seedling tray until damp soil squeezed between his fingers. He pictured every bucket he had hauled, every weed he had pulled from neighboring plots. Now the committee stood nearby, avoiding his eyes. “You knew I was here.” His jaw ached from clenching it. He kicked the sign loose, then stopped himself from snapping it across his knee. Instead, he planted his seedlings along the neglected fence, each thrust of the trowel hard enough to strike sparks from stone.

Mei entered the community garden through a gate painted brick-red beneath a pale red morning sky. She carried a red canvas bag containing crimson seed packets, scarlet twine, and a rust-colored trowel. Along the central path, red gravel bordered beds framed with dark red cedar boards. Mei measured a row beside ruby chard stems and pressed red bean seeds into the brown-red soil. At the next plot, two gardeners filled vermilion watering cans from a pump with a maroon handle. A child sorted red plant labels on a carmine table while an older gardener stacked coral-red pots beneath a red awning. Mei tied the tomato vines with scarlet twine, then placed a red label at the end of each row. Near the shed, a red wheelbarrow held radishes, red onions, and folded burgundy netting for the berry bed. When the work period ended, Mei rinsed the rust-red trowel, returned the crimson packets to her red bag, and left through the brick-red gate.

Omar entered the community garden through the side gate and placed a canvas bag beside the tool shed. He took out gloves, a small trowel, and a packet of bean seeds. Along the central path, several neighbors worked among the plots, pulling weeds and tying stems to wooden stakes. Omar stopped at his assigned bed and cleared dry leaves from the soil. He loosened the ground with the trowel, made a row of shallow holes, and dropped seeds into them. After covering the row, he carried a watering can to the outdoor tap. Someone waiting there said, “The hose is beside the fence.” Omar nodded, filled the can, and returned to his plot. Water darkened the soil in narrow patches. He checked the labels beside the herbs, trimmed a few basil stalks, and placed them in his bag. Before leaving, he rinsed the trowel, hung the watering can on its hook, and latched the gate behind him.

Omar worked in a community garden beside the harbor, where seawater tapped the stone wall below the plots. Each morning, he checked the tide chart before carrying compost past rows of beans, kale, and salt-tolerant herbs. Gulls crossed above the coastline while neighbors filled watering cans from a rain tank shaped like a ship’s barrel. Omar spread seaweed mulch around the tomatoes, removing shells and small pieces of driftwood as he went. Beyond the fence, fishing boats moved across the bay, and their wakes reached the shore in narrow waves. A gardener pointed toward a bed of coastal strawberries and said, “The soil needs more sand.” Omar measured a bucket, mixed sand into the earth, and recorded the amount while crabs moved between rocks near the seawall.
