At noon, the group ate beside the lettuce beds as seals surfaced beyond the harbor buoys. Omar ended the day by rinsing tools near the coast and storing them in a shed facing the open sea.

Omar arrived at the community garden with a notebook and measured the planting beds. Four beds were each 6 meters long, so he recorded 4 × 6 = 24 meters of rows. He counted 38 tomato seedlings and added 14 pepper seedlings, writing 38 + 14 = 52 seedlings. After placing 9 damaged pots beside the shed, he revised the pot count from 67 to 58 because 67 − 9 = 58. A neighbor brought 36 wooden stakes. Omar divided them among 6 plots, calculating 36 ÷ 6 = 6 stakes per plot. He then marked spaces for beans. Three rows held 8 plants each, giving 3 × 8 = 24 plants. Along the path, 15 paving stones joined 27 existing stones, so 15 + 27 = 42 stones bordered the beds. Before leaving, Omar split 48 liters of collected rainwater across 8 barrels: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 liters per barrel. He closed the notebook and stored the tools.

Morning light fell across the raised beds of the community garden, where bean vines climbed twine and marigolds bordered the paths. Zainab arrived carrying a tin of saved sunflower seeds for the oldest gardener, who had taught her to loosen roots with her fingers and leave water for birds. His plot stood untouched. A folded notice hung from the gate, announcing that he had died during the night. Zainab read it twice, then lowered herself onto the damp path. The seed tin slipped from her hand, scattering black shells into the mud. Around her, volunteers spoke quietly and continued watering, but she could not move. She pictured his cracked hands pressing seedlings into soil, his straw hat bobbing between rows. Her throat closed, and each breath scraped. At last, she gathered the seeds one by one, though tears blurred them into dark specks. In his empty bed, she planted every seed, leaving the tin beside his trowel.

The community garden occupied a narrow lot between brick apartments and the railway embankment. Omar arrived at dawn carrying tomato seedlings for the raised bed he shared with an elderly gardener. For three summers, the man had taught him to pinch suckers, save seeds, and read rain in the undersides of leaves. That morning, the gate stood open, but the man’s battered watering can remained beneath the tool shed window. A neighbor approached and quietly explained that he had died during the night. Omar set down the seedlings. One pot tipped, spilling black soil across his shoes. “He was coming today,” Omar said. He waited beside the unfinished bed, staring at the empty path. His throat tightened until each breath scraped. He pressed both hands into the earth they had turned together, remembering the packet of bean seeds still tucked in his pocket. By noon, he had planted every seed, though tears kept dropping into the furrows. He placed the watering can at the head of the row and could not make himself leave.

Morning light fell across the raised beds of the community garden, where bean vines climbed wooden frames beside rows of tomatoes. Zainab knelt between two plots, pressing her fingers into soil that had been dry and stubborn for weeks. Neighbors carried watering cans, children gathered weeds, and an older gardener adjusted the rain barrel. Together they had planted, mulched, and hauled compost, hoping the struggling seedlings would recover. When Zainab lifted a broad squash leaf, she found three golden blossoms and, beneath them, a green fruit as long as her hand. She stared, then called, “Come and see.” Everyone crowded around. More discoveries followed: peppers beneath tangled stems, strawberries glowing near the path, and dozens of beans ready to pick. Zainab sprang upright, laughing until she had to catch her breath. Her cheeks ached from grinning. She filled a basket, passed vegetables to waiting hands, and thought the whole garden seemed to be answering their work with abundance.

When the neighborhood lost power at 8:15, Dmitri set a notebook beside the window and counted the lit apartments across the street. Before the outage, 24 windows had shown light; afterward, 24 - 20 = 4 remained lit by battery lamps. He checked his supplies: 6 candles with 5 hours each gave 6 × 5 = 30 candle-hours. His apartment had 3 rooms, so 30 ÷ 3 = 10 hours per room if he divided them evenly. He placed 2 candles in the kitchen, 1 in the hall, and 3 on the table; 2 + 1 + 3 = 6. Dmitri timed passing vehicles: 7 went east and 5 went west, for 7 + 5 = 12 vehicles. After 46 minutes, power returned. From 9:01 to 9:25, he observed 24 minutes of restored service, and 46 + 24 = 70 minutes had elapsed since 8:15. He closed the notebook, extinguished the candles, and reset two clocks.

The community garden stretched between two apartment blocks, its raised beds bright with tomatoes, beans, and marigolds. Zainab knelt beside the herb patch, loosening soil around a row of mint, while several neighbors filled watering cans nearby. A sharp hiss rose behind the tool shed. At first, she mistook it for a sprinkler, but then the sour stink of gas rolled across the path. Someone dropped a trowel. Zainab saw a split in the pipe beside the shed, where an old heater was connected. Her pulse hammered against her throat. A neighbor reached for the shed’s light switch. “Don’t touch it,” Zainab said. Her voice cracked. She backed away, knees shaking, imagining one spark turning the beds, fences, and gathered families into flame. The hiss grew louder. Her fingers fumbled twice before she managed to call emergency services. She ordered everyone toward the street, counting each person through shallow breaths, never taking her eyes from the pipe until sirens approached.

Omar entered the community garden through a red gate and recorded the date on a crimson clipboard. He inspected rows marked by brick-red tiles, where tomatoes, red chard, and scarlet runner beans grew beneath copper-colored trellises. He then carried a maroon watering can between beds edged with russet boards, pouring measured amounts around each plant. Near the vermilion shed, two volunteers sorted ruby radishes into red plastic crates while Omar counted empty seed packets. A cardinal-red wheelbarrow stood beside a pile of reddish mulch, and he used its red-handled shovel to spread the material evenly. Under a striped red canopy, he updated a burgundy map showing plots, paths, and the shared herb section. At midday, sunlight passed through red fabric panels, laying rectangular rose-colored patches across the gravel path. Omar rinsed clay-red pots at a tap, stacked them on a crimson shelf, and checked the red twine supporting young vines. Before leaving, he latched the red gate, placed the clipboard in a dark-red cabinet, and left the garden arranged as scheduled.

Saturday sunlight fell across the raised beds of the community garden, striping the paths between rows of beans and marigolds. Zainab arrived with seedlings she had raised for weeks, only to find her assigned plot fenced off and marked for a new member. At the shed, the coordinator shrugged and said the printed map overruled her handwritten receipt. “You can take the corner by the bins.” Zainab stared at the weed-choked patch, then at the thriving bed she had composted, edged, and watered all spring. Someone was already pressing tomatoes into her soil. Heat surged up her neck. Her jaw locked so hard it ached, and her fingers crushed a paper seed pot into pulp. They had taken her labor, then offered her rubbish. She marched to the noticeboard, pinned her receipt over the map, and rang the brass meeting bell until every gardener looked up. “No one plants another seed until this is settled.” She planted herself before the gate, arms crossed, while dirt slid from her clenched fists.

Zainab tended the community garden beside a harbor where seawater tapped the stone wall. Each morning, she measured the tide before opening the gate for other gardeners from the coastal neighborhood. Salt wind crossed the vegetable beds, and mesh screens protected lettuce leaves from sea spray. Zainab mixed kelp into the compost while fishing boats moved between red and green buoys. Along the shoreline, gulls searched among shells as volunteers planted beans in raised wooden boxes. “The tide is turning,” one gardener said, carrying a bucket rinsed with seawater. Zainab recorded the time, then checked a channel that guided collected rainwater past beds shaped like small islands. Beyond the fence, seals rested on a harbor platform while ferries traced white lines across the bay. At midday, the group divided radishes and herbs beside a mural of whales. Zainab stored the tools in a shed facing the coast, and the evening tide covered the lowest harbor steps.

Morning sunlight crossed the raised beds of the community garden, catching on wet leaves and bamboo stakes. Emeka knelt beside the tomato plants he had tended for months, examining stems that had once drooped thinly against the soil. Neighbors arrived carrying baskets, gloves, and watering cans, while children searched beneath broad leaves. Then a child drew back a branch, revealing clusters of ripe red tomatoes, more than anyone had expected. Soon beans filled one basket, peppers filled another, and the repaired rain barrel poured clear water without leaking. Emeka sprang to his feet. His breath came fast, and a wide grin pulled at his cheeks until they ached. He clapped his muddy hands, laughed from deep in his chest, and spun once between the beds. “Look at what we grew,” he said. Around him, neighbors began dividing the harvest for nearby families. Emeka lifted a heavy basket, marveling at its weight, and felt as if sunlight had opened inside him.

Zainab entered the community garden through a red gate and signed the clipboard with a crimson pencil. Along the brick-red path, she carried a scarlet bucket toward the tomato beds. Red twine marked each row, and burgundy labels listed planting dates beside dark red stakes. She loosened russet soil around radishes whose red shoulders rose above the ground. Nearby, two gardeners spread a maroon cloth across a table and sorted red bean seeds into clay-red bowls. Zainab filled a vermilion watering can from a tap mounted on a red post. She poured measured circles around ruby chard, red cabbage, and copper-red peppers. Under a faded crimson awning, another gardener recorded the harvest on pink-red paper. Zainab placed six tomatoes in a red crate, then brushed brick dust from its corners. At noon, red light passed through translucent panels on the tool shed. She returned the scarlet bucket, closed the red gate, and left the garden along the rust-colored pavement.

Zainab entered the community garden with a clipboard and counted 18 tomato plants, 12 pepper plants, and 10 bean plants. She added 18 + 12 + 10 = 40 plants in the eastern beds. Two volunteers removed 7 damaged stakes from a stack of 32, so she recorded 32 - 7 = 25 usable stakes. Along the fence, 6 plots each measured 4 meters, and Zainab calculated 6 × 4 = 24 meters of planting space. A water barrel held 48 liters. Dividing it equally among 8 beds gave 48 ÷ 8 = 6 liters per bed. She placed 3 rows of 9 lettuce seedlings, writing 3 × 9 = 27 seedlings. After 5 were moved to another bed, 27 - 5 = 22 remained. At the compost station, gardeners delivered 14 buckets in the morning and 11 later, making 14 + 11 = 25 buckets. Zainab divided 25 buckets among 5 bins, so each received 25 ÷ 5 = 5 buckets. She closed the clipboard and rinsed the measuring jug.

Morning light spread across the raised beds of the community garden, where tomatoes climbed wooden stakes beside rows of beans. Emeka carried a watering can toward the corner plot he had tended with his father for six summers. He expected to find the broad pumpkin leaves they had planted before the hospital stay, but the plot was bare. A notice on the fence explained that untended beds had been cleared and reassigned. Fresh seedlings stood in the turned soil, each marked with another gardener’s tag. Emeka set down the can. Water sloshed over his shoes, but he did not move. His father’s old hand trowel, hidden beneath the pumpkin vines, was gone too. “I should have come sooner,” he whispered. He crouched beside the fence, pressing both hands into the earth as his throat tightened. The funeral had been three days earlier. Until then, he had imagined the pumpkins continuing without them. Now even that small living trace had vanished, and his shoulders shook while the garden carried on around him.

Emeka arrived at the community garden after breakfast and opened the wooden gate. He carried a small trowel, a coil of string, and an empty basket. Several gardeners were already working among the plots. One person filled a watering can at the tap, while another pulled weeds beside the path. Emeka walked to his assigned bed and set his tools on a flat stone. He loosened the soil around the bean plants, removed dry leaves, and placed them in the compost bin. Then he tied two leaning stems to bamboo stakes. A gardener passing with a bucket said, “The tap is running slowly today.” Emeka nodded and continued along the row. He checked the herbs, picked a few mature leaves, and put them in his basket. Near the fence, sparrows searched the mulch for seeds. Emeka swept loose soil from the path, rinsed his trowel, closed the gate behind him, and walked home before lunch.

Zainab arrived at the community garden after breakfast, carrying a canvas bag with gloves, string, and a small trowel. She unlocked the tool shed, set the watering cans beside the tap, and checked the noticeboard for the weekly list. A volunteer was already loosening soil around the bean poles, while another swept gravel from the path. Zainab weeded the herb bed, placing dandelions and dry stems in a bucket. She tied a leaning tomato plant to its stake, then spread compost beneath the leaves. Near the fence, she watched a bee move among lavender flowers and heard a bus pass beyond the houses. At midday, she rinsed the trowel and filled the birdbath from a hose. Several neighbors entered with seed packets and paper cups. Zainab handed over the shed key, folded an empty sack, and wrote “mulch needed” on the board. Before leaving, she closed the gate and brushed loose soil from her shoes.

Rows of tomatoes, beans, and marigolds filled the community garden beneath the late-afternoon sun. Emeka knelt beside a raised bed, winding twine around a leaning pepper plant while neighbors carried watering cans between plots. A sharp crack came from the old shed. He looked up as its rusted door swung outward and a cloud of wasps poured from the gap beneath the roof. Someone dropped a bucket. The insects spread across the path, driving gardeners toward the gate. Emeka started after them, then heard a child crying behind the bean trellis. His throat tightened. Wasps struck his shirt and circled his face as he ran back, every wingbeat sounding like a warning inside his skull. “Stay low,” he said, barely forcing out the words. He covered the child with his jacket and crawled toward the fence, convinced the swarm would engulf them before they reached it. His hands shook so violently he could hardly lift the loose wire. At last they rolled under, and Emeka lay gasping, staring at the black cloud above the garden.

At dawn, rows of tomatoes and beans filled the community garden behind the library. Emeka arrived carrying seedlings he had raised for six weeks, only to find his assigned plot stripped bare. A new wooden sign claimed it for a council member’s relative, and his compost, tools, and irrigation hose lay heaped beside the fence. The coordinator glanced at a clipboard and said, “The allocation was revised.” Emeka pointed to the signed agreement in his pocket, but the coordinator shrugged and turned away. Heat surged up his neck. His jaw locked until his teeth hurt, and he drove the shovel into the path so hard the blade rang against stone. Six weeks of watering under grow lamps, three Saturdays repairing the shared beds, and they expected him to swallow this theft. He dragged the hose back across the garden, crushing the edge of the usurper’s neat mulch. Then he planted his seedlings in the unused central bed, posted his agreement above them, and stood watch with both fists clenched.

Emeka entered the community garden through a gate painted brick red. Red gravel marked the central path, bordered by rows of crimson lettuce and ruby chard. He carried a scarlet watering can to a bed framed with red cedar planks. Nearby, volunteers tied tomato vines to rust-red stakes with strips of maroon cloth. Emeka measured the soil beneath a red plastic marker and wrote the number in a burgundy notebook. Under a vermilion shade cloth, several neighbors sorted radishes into red crates. “This row needs water,” one person said. Emeka directed the scarlet spout along the dark red mulch until each plant received the listed amount. A shed with coral-red doors held clay pots, red twine, and packets labeled for red peppers. At noon, muted red light passed through the canopy and crossed the shared tables. Emeka placed three ripe tomatoes in a crimson basket, returned the tools to their red hooks, and updated the garden chart with a carmine pencil. Then he left by the brick-red gate.

Emeka entered the community garden and counted 12 beds along the fence and 9 beside the path. He recorded 12 + 9 = 21 beds on the supply board. Each bed had 6 rows, so he calculated 21 × 6 = 126 rows. Volunteers had planted 98 rows, leaving 126 − 98 = 28 rows unplanted. Emeka divided those rows among 7 workers: 28 ÷ 7 = 4 rows per worker. Near the shed, he arranged 5 trays containing 8 seedlings each, which gave 5 × 8 = 40 seedlings. After placing 27 seedlings, he noted 40 − 27 = 13 remaining. Two rain barrels held 60 liters and 45 liters, for 60 + 45 = 105 liters. Using 5 liters on each of 21 beds required 5 × 21 = 105 liters. He then measured three paths, each 14 meters long, totaling 3 × 14 = 42 meters, and marked every 6 meters, making 42 ÷ 6 = 7 sections.

Emeka tended the community garden beside a harbor where seawater tapped the stone quay. Each morning, he carried compost past moored fishing boats and spread it beneath rows of coastal kale. Gulls crossed above the allotments while small waves folded against the pilings. At low tide, Emeka collected rinsed seaweed from the exposed shoreline and added measured layers to the soil. Other gardeners planted beans, onions, and tomatoes as ferries moved across the bay. A wooden sign near the herb beds listed watering times according to tides, since salt spray reached the outer plots at high water. “The mulch goes here,” Emeka said, pointing toward a bed bordered with shells. Crabs moved between rocks beyond the fence while he tied cucumber vines to stakes made from retired oars. At noon, a cargo ship sounded its horn offshore, and the gardeners paused before returning to their tools. Emeka finished by rinsing the spade at a freshwater tap, watching silver fish turn beneath the harbor surface, and recording the day’s harvest in the shared ledger.

Saturday sunlight fell across the steel counters of the neighborhood cooking school. Martha tied her apron and studied the recipe for cheese soufflé while the instructor demonstrated each careful fold. Her first mixture collapsed into a lumpy puddle, but she started again, whisking the egg whites until they formed shining peaks. This time, she turned the bowl slowly and lifted the batter as gently as cloth. When the oven timer rang, Martha crouched beside the glass door. The soufflé had climbed above its dish, golden and airy, without a crack in its crown. She sprang upright, clapped both floury hands, and left white prints on her cheeks when she covered her mouth. Laughter burst from her until she had to grip the counter. “It rose,” she said. The instructor cut a serving, and steam curled from the tender center. Martha tasted it, closed her eyes, and bounced once on her toes. She wanted to make a dozen more and carry them to everyone she knew.

Copper pans hung above six steel worktables in the evening cooking class. Martha tied on her apron and began slicing onions for the instructor’s winter stew. Her phone vibrated beside the flour canister, although she had silenced it before class. She ignored the first call, then answered when it rang again. Her sister’s voice came thinly through the speaker. Their mother had died ten minutes earlier, before Martha could reach the hospital or say goodbye. The knife slipped from Martha’s fingers and struck the board. Around her, stock simmered and classmates stirred pots, unaware. “I have to go,” she whispered. She untied the apron, but the scent of rosemary stopped her. Her mother had rubbed rosemary between her palms whenever they cooked together, scattering it over potatoes while Martha stole crisp pieces from the pan. Martha crushed a sprig in her fist. Her knees folded, and she crouched beside the table, pressing both hands to her mouth as tears fell onto the tiled floor.

Martha arrived at the cooking class and hung her coat beside the door. She chose a station near the window, washed her hands, and placed an apron over her clothes. The instructor reviewed the recipe for vegetable soup and pointed out the knives, pans, and cutting boards. Martha collected an onion, two carrots, a potato, celery, and several herbs. She peeled the vegetables, cut them into even pieces, and placed them in separate bowls. Around her, other students worked at their stations and rinsed utensils in the sinks. Martha warmed oil in a pot, added the onion, and stirred it with a wooden spoon. She added the remaining vegetables, poured in stock, and covered the pot. While the soup simmered, she wiped the counter and washed the knife. The instructor checked each pot and suggested adding pepper. Martha followed the suggestion, filled a small bowl, and tasted the soup. At the end, she stored the recipe sheet in her bag, cleaned her station, removed her apron, and left.

Copper pans hung above six steel counters in the evening cooking class. Martha sliced onions while the instructor demonstrated how to sear chicken in a shallow pan. When another student tipped meat into hot oil, flames leaped toward the ceiling and caught the sleeve of a hanging apron. The instructor smothered the pan, but the apron burned upward, carrying fire to a rack of towels. Smoke rolled across the room. Martha reached for the nearest extinguisher and squeezed; nothing came out. Her breath snagged. The exit lay beyond the spreading flames, and the second door refused to open when a student shoved it. “It’s locked,” someone said. Martha’s hands began shaking so violently that she dropped the metal cylinder. Heat tightened the skin on her face. She imagined the smoke filling her lungs, the doors staying shut, the ceiling collapsing. Crouching, she crawled beneath the smoke, found the extinguisher’s safety pin still inserted, yanked it free, and sprayed until the path to the exit cleared.

On Tuesday evening, copper pans hung above six flour-dusted workstations in the community kitchen. Martha measured saffron and folded butter into her risotto while her assigned partner scrolled through messages. When the instructor tasted the dish, the partner stepped forward and described “our” careful technique. Martha opened her mouth, but the instructor awarded the partner a ribbon and told Martha she should contribute more next time. Heat surged up her neck. Her fingers clamped around the wooden spoon until her knuckles blanched. She had spent forty minutes stirring while that thief had barely touched an onion. “I made every part of it,” she said. The instructor waved her aside and began the next demonstration. Martha’s pulse hammered. She yanked off her apron, scattering flour across the counter, then seized the recipe card bearing her notes. Before leaving, she scraped the prizewinning risotto into the rubbish bin, ribbon and all, while the class stared in silence.

Martha attended a cooking class in a tiled kitchen with eleven other participants. The instructor assigned three trays of rolls, with eight rolls per tray, so Martha calculated 3 × 8 = 24 rolls. She measured 600 grams of flour and divided it among four bowls: 600 ÷ 4 = 150 grams per bowl. Next, she combined 150 grams with 35 grams of oats, writing 150 + 35 = 185 grams beside the recipe. The mixture required 90 milliliters of water, but 18 milliliters remained in the cup, so 90 − 18 = 72 milliliters entered the bowl. “Knead for six minutes,” the instructor said. Martha tracked the time as 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 minutes. She cut the dough into twelve portions, placing four portions on each of three pans because 12 ÷ 3 = 4. After baking, two rolls were set aside for demonstration, leaving 24 − 2 = 22 rolls. Martha recorded the totals, washed two bowls and one cup, and stacked 2 + 1 = 3 clean items on the shelf.

Martha attended a cooking class in a low building beside the harbor, where seawater tapped the stone wall with each passing wave. Through the windows, fishing boats crossed the inlet while gulls circled above the tide. The instructor placed mussels, seaweed, cod, and coastal herbs on a long wooden table. Martha rinsed the mussels in salted water as a ferry moved between two points of the coastline. She sliced the cod into even pieces while sunlight shifted across the calm bay. “Keep the broth below a boil,” the instructor said over the sound of waves against the pier. Martha added kelp stock, potatoes, and cream to a steel pot shaped like a small ship’s basin. Around her, other students measured spices while seals surfaced beyond the harbor buoys. The class carried their bowls onto the pier when the tide reached the lower steps. Martha ate the chowder beside a coil of rope, watching a cargo vessel follow the channel toward the open sea.

Copper pans hung above the long counter, and afternoon sun striped the tiled floor of the cooking classroom. Arjun tied his apron and watched the instructor demonstrate how to fold dough around a spiced potato filling. His first dumpling split, scattering peas across the board, but he gathered another circle of dough and tried again. He pinched more gently, turning the parcel between his fingers until its pleats formed a neat crown. When the dumplings came out of the steamer, his remained sealed and upright. He bit into one, and the thin wrapper gave way to fragrant cumin, ginger, and warm potato. The instructor nodded and said, “That is exactly right.” Heat rushed into Arjun’s cheeks. He broke into a wide grin, then laughed so suddenly that flour puffed from his apron. His pulse danced as he arranged the remaining dumplings on a plate. He imagined making them for his family, each pleat just as perfect, and could hardly keep his feet still beneath the counter.

The cooking classroom held six steel workstations beneath rows of copper pans. Arjun arrived early, measured every spice, and simmered his sauce until it gleamed. When the instructor tasted it, he nodded and carried the bowl to the demonstration table. Minutes later, another student presented the same sauce as her own, and the instructor praised her balanced seasoning. Arjun raised his hand, but the instructor waved him down. “We have no time for disputes.” Heat crawled up Arjun’s neck. His jaw locked as the student accepted applause beside his untouched workstation, where his handwritten recipe still lay. He gripped his wooden spoon until the handle creaked. They had watched him cook it; they knew. Yet his work had become someone else’s triumph because speaking up was inconvenient. He shoved the spice jars into a straight line, each striking the counter hard. Then he lifted his recipe, walked to the demonstration table, and set it beside the stolen bowl. “Check the stains and timestamps.” The room went silent.

The cooking class occupied a narrow kitchen above a crowded market. Arjun stood at a steel counter, slicing onions while the instructor demonstrated how to flambé a pan of sauce. When his turn came, he tipped brandy into the skillet and leaned toward the burner. A blue flame raced up the bottle’s neck. The instructor knocked it from his hand, but it struck the floor, spilling fire beneath the counters. Smoke rolled toward the ceiling, and someone shouted for everyone to leave. Arjun’s knife clattered from his fingers. His chest clenched; each breath scraped his throat. The exit lay beyond the burning spill, and the second door would not open. He pictured the gas cylinders beside the stove rupturing, tearing the room apart. His knees shook so violently that he gripped the counter to remain upright. Then the instructor smothered the flames with a heavy blanket. Even outside, Arjun stared at the windows, pulse hammering, certain an explosion would still come.

The cooking classroom held six steel counters beneath rows of copper pans. Arjun unfolded his mother’s stained recipe card and set it beside the flour. The instructor had asked everyone to bring a family dish, so he chose the card he had avoided since the funeral. As butter melted, her handwriting guided him through each step, its slant recalling mornings when she tapped the spoon against his wrist and told him to taste twice. A student reaching for salt knocked over a bowl. Water rushed across the counter, soaking the card before Arjun could lift it. The blue ink bled into shapeless clouds. “I’m sorry,” the student whispered. Arjun pressed the paper between towels, but the final lines vanished under his thumbs. His chest tightened. He turned from the stove, covering his mouth as tears dropped onto his apron. The sauce scorched behind him. He could no longer remember whether she had added cumin first or last, and the missing order felt like losing her voice a second time.

Martha entered the cooking classroom beneath red ceiling lamps and placed her notebook beside a row of crimson bowls. The instructor distributed scarlet aprons while six participants arranged red peppers, ruby tomatoes, and radishes on vermilion boards. Martha tied her carmine apron and measured paprika from a red tin into a terracotta dish. “Slice the peppers evenly,” the instructor said, pointing with a red silicone spatula. Under the russet pendant light, Martha cut each pepper into narrow strips and set them on a maroon tray. A participant passed her a red colander, and she rinsed cherry tomatoes over a basin lined with burgundy tiles. Martha stirred the vegetables in a copper-red pan, then added lentils from a brick-red jar. Rose-tinted vapor drifted toward a rack of red ladles and dark crimson towels. The mixture gradually became a garnet sauce flecked with paprika. Martha spooned equal portions onto red ceramic plates and added strips of scarlet pepper. At the red counter, the class recorded cooking times in notebooks with maroon covers. Martha washed her utensils and hung the red apron beside the others.

Arjun attended a cooking class in a whitewashed kitchen beside the harbor, where seawater tapped the stone quay below. Through open windows, he watched fishing boats cross the bay while an instructor arranged mussels, seaweed, and silver-skinned mackerel on a long table. The tide moved between dock posts as Arjun measured rice and rinsed it with fresh water. Gulls circled above the coastline while he sliced fennel into narrow strips. The instructor pointed toward a pot and said, “Add the broth slowly.” Beyond the stove, sunlight shifted across the waves, and a ferry passed between two green buoys. Arjun stirred the rice, then folded in chopped seaweed as small crabs moved among rocks near the harbor wall. Other students cleaned shellfish while nets dried on a nearby trawler. When the mackerel had cooked, Arjun placed it beside the rice and added fennel. The class ate at a terrace facing the channel, where seals surfaced near an anchored sailboat. Afterward, Arjun washed his utensils while the outgoing tide exposed bands of dark sand.

Copper pans hung above the long counter in the cooking school’s tiled kitchen. Sana tied her apron and watched the instructor demonstrate how to fold butter into pastry dough without warming it. Her first batch tore, leaking butter across the tray, but she started again, cooling her hands under tap water and counting each careful turn. When the oven door finally opened, six golden croissants stood in perfect curled layers. Sana stared as their crisp shells crackled in the heat. She lifted one, split it, and saw a honeycomb of airy pockets inside. “You did it,” the instructor said. Warmth rushed through Sana’s chest and up her neck. She laughed, then covered her mouth, unable to stop grinning. The first bite scattered flakes over her apron and filled her mouth with butter and steam. She bounced once on her toes, hugged the tray against herself, and imagined making dozens for everyone she knew. Even the failed dough seemed worth celebrating now.

Copper pans hung above the cooking classroom, and six stoves lined the tiled walls. Sana rolled dough for the almond pastries her grandmother had taught her to make, pressing each circle with the rim of a chipped cup. While the pastries baked, her phone vibrated against the counter. She wiped flour from her fingers and answered. Her brother’s voice came thinly through the speaker. “She died this morning.” The timer rang, but Sana did not move. Heat swelled from the oven, carrying the scent of almonds and orange blossom, exactly as it had filled her grandmother’s kitchen every winter. Her knees folded, and she gripped the counter until someone pulled out a chair. When the instructor set the browned pastries before her, Sana broke one open. Steam brushed her face. She remembered wrinkled hands guiding hers, a cup of tea cooling beside the dough, and a promise to visit next week. The pastry crumbled in her palm as tears spotted the recipe card.

Arjun arrived at the community kitchen shortly before the cooking class began. He hung his coat on a hook, washed his hands, and took a place beside a steel worktable. The instructor set out bowls, knives, onions, herbs, beans, and a tray of flatbread. Arjun watched a brief demonstration, then sliced an onion and chopped the herbs into small pieces. He added oil to a pan, stirred the onion with a wooden spoon, and waited while it softened. Around him, other participants worked at their stations, and the room filled with the sounds of knives, taps, and running water. Arjun poured in the beans, scattered the herbs across the pan, and followed the instructor’s directions for seasoning. While the mixture warmed, he wiped the worktable and stacked the used bowls near the sink. He spooned the food onto flatbread, folded it, and ate it at the table. Afterward, he rinsed his utensils, dried them, returned them to the counter, collected his coat, and left with the others.

Copper pans hung above six flour-dusted stations in the evening cooking class. Sana had spent an hour folding butter into pastry, following every instruction while her partner wandered away to chat. When the instructor inspected their tart, the partner stepped forward and claimed the careful layers as her own. “She only washed the bowls,” she said. The instructor praised her and placed a blue ribbon beside the tart. Heat surged up Sana’s neck. Her fingers locked around the handle of a rolling pin until her knuckles blanched. She pictured the wasted butter, the repeated turns, the partner watching from across the room while Sana worked. Then the instructor ordered Sana to clean their station because “the winner” needed photographs. A bitter pulse hammered behind her eyes. Sana set down the pin with a hard crack, pulled out her phone, and displayed the time-stamped pictures she had taken during each stage. “Check who is holding the dough,” she said. Silence spread. Sana took the ribbon, pinned it to her apron, and left every dirty bowl for her partner.

Sana stood at a steel counter in a crowded cooking classroom while rain tapped the high windows. The instructor demonstrated how to sear chicken, and Sana set her pan over the blue flame. Oil shimmered across its surface. When she lowered the meat, grease spat onto the burner, and fire leaped up the side of the pan. Someone knocked over a bottle of oil while stepping back. A bright stream crept toward the stove. Sana’s breath stopped. Her hands shook so violently that the tongs clattered to the floor, and her heart hammered against her ribs. The flames climbed toward the hood, filling the room with black smoke. She pictured the oil igniting, the doorway vanishing behind fire. “Turn off the gas,” the instructor said. Sana reached for the knob, but heat drove her back. She snatched a metal lid from the counter and slammed it over the pan. The flames collapsed beneath it as another student dragged the spilled oil away. Sana remained against the wall, knees buckling, unable to unclench her jaw.

Arjun entered the cooking class and placed 3 tomatoes, 5 onions, and a bowl on his station. He calculated 3 + 5 = 8 vegetables before washing them. The instructor provided 12 mushrooms, and Arjun removed 4 stems, leaving 12 - 4 = 8 whole mushrooms. He cut each of 6 carrots into 8 pieces, producing 6 × 8 = 48 pieces. Dividing those among 4 trays gave 48 ÷ 4 = 12 carrot pieces per tray. For the sauce, he combined 250 milliliters of stock with 150 milliliters of tomato liquid, so 250 + 150 = 400 milliliters. He used 120 milliliters, leaving 400 - 120 = 280 milliliters. He formed 7 dough portions weighing 60 grams each; 7 × 60 = 420 grams. After baking, he divided 24 rolls among 6 students, calculating 24 ÷ 6 = 4 rolls each. Arjun recorded the quantities, cleaned his board, and stored the remaining ingredients.

Sana arrived at the cooking class and placed her bag beneath a wooden bench. An instructor handed out aprons and directed everyone toward the sinks. Sana washed her hands, tied back her hair, and stood at an open section of the counter. The lesson covered vegetable soup and flatbread. She peeled a carrot, trimmed a leek, and cut both into small pieces. Around her, other students worked at separate boards while pans rested on the stovetop. The instructor demonstrated how to knead dough, then moved between the counters to check its texture. Sana added flour to her bowl, poured in water, and mixed the ingredients with a spoon. She kneaded the dough, covered it with a cloth, and returned to the soup. After the vegetables softened, she stirred in stock and herbs. She rolled the dough into thin rounds and cooked them in a dry pan. At the end, everyone washed utensils, wiped the counters, and packed portions into containers. Sana removed her apron, collected her bag, and left.

Wei stepped off the first flight and followed the signs toward the connecting gates. His next departure was listed on a screen near the concourse entrance. He stopped at a restroom, then filled his water bottle at a fountain. Along the walkway, shop windows displayed headphones, magazines, and travel pillows. A cleaner pushed a cart between rows of seats, while passengers checked phones or watched aircraft through the glass. Wei bought a plain sandwich and tea from a counter. “Receipt?” the cashier asked. “No, thanks,” Wei said. He carried the tray to an empty table, ate, and placed the wrapper in a bin. Afterward, he walked to his gate and confirmed the destination on the display. He plugged his phone into an outlet, skimmed several pages of a newspaper, and listened as routine announcements passed overhead. When boarding began, he unplugged the cable, put the newspaper on a nearby rack, joined the line, and presented his pass.

Sana entered the cooking classroom through a red door and placed her notebook beside a crimson cutting board. Red curtains filtered the afternoon light, laying ruby rectangles across the red-tiled counter. An instructor in a scarlet apron arranged tomatoes, red peppers, radishes, and a bowl of paprika before the group. Sana tied on a burgundy apron and measured red lentils into a copper pot painted with vermilion bands. “Slice the peppers thinly,” the instructor said, pointing with a red-handled knife. Sana cut the glossy peppers into narrow strips, then diced tomatoes over a carmine tray. Around her, several students stirred matching pots with dark red spoons. She added paprika, tomato paste, and a pinch of rose-colored salt from a red ceramic dish. The mixture thickened beneath the ruby light while she recorded the timing in red ink. “Add the lentils now,” said the instructor. Sana poured them in, stirred twice, and set the finished dish in a brick-red bowl beside folded maroon napkins.

Arjun entered the cooking studio beneath a red glass pendant and placed his notebook beside a crimson cutting board. On each counter, a scarlet bowl held tomatoes, red peppers, and radishes, while burgundy towels hung from brass hooks. The instructor demonstrated a ruby-colored sauce in a red enamel pot, measuring paprika with a vermilion spoon. Arjun diced the tomatoes on the crimson board and slid them into a maroon pan. Under the red pendant light, he stirred the mixture until its shade shifted from coral to brick red. A classmate passed him a red ceramic jar, and he added a spoonful of pepper paste. “Fold in the beans,” the instructor said, pointing toward a bowl striped in red and white. Arjun folded in the beans, arranged roasted red pepper strips across the surface, and wiped the rim with a russet cloth. The class served portions on dark-red plates beside glasses filled with red berry tea. Arjun copied the recipe into his red notebook and washed the scarlet utensils.

Sana attended a cooking class in a tiled kitchen with eleven other participants. The instructor placed 24 tomatoes on a counter, and Sana divided them among 6 stations: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 tomatoes per station. Her recipe required 3 onions for each of 2 pots, so she calculated 3 × 2 = 6 onions. She chopped 8 carrots, then removed 2 pieces with damaged ends: 8 − 2 = 6 usable carrots. For the broth, she combined 5 cups of water with 3 cups of stock, making 5 + 3 = 8 cups. “Measure twice,” the instructor said. Sana weighed 600 grams of flour and split it into 4 bowls: 600 ÷ 4 = 150 grams each. She added 7 spoonfuls of herbs to one pot and 5 to another, totaling 7 + 5 = 12 spoonfuls. After 40 minutes, she subtracted 15 minutes of simmering from the schedule, leaving 40 − 15 = 25 minutes for baking. The class then portioned the dishes onto plates.

Sana attended a cooking class in a low building beside the harbor, where fishing boats shifted with the tide. Through open windows, seawater tapped the stone quay, and gulls crossed above the coastline. The instructor placed mussels, seaweed, potatoes, and silver-scaled fish on a counter facing the waves. Sana rinsed the mussels while a ferry moved across the bay beyond her cutting board. “Slice the seaweed thinly,” the instructor said as foam gathered along the harbor wall. She cut the kelp into narrow ribbons, then stirred them into a pot of stock made from fish bones and seawater salt. Around her, the other students measured herbs while sails passed between two coastal headlands. Sana arranged fish fillets in a pan and watched the tide expose dark rocks covered with barnacles. The class added mussels to the simmering broth as seals surfaced near a buoy outside. When the dish was ready, Sana carried her bowl to a table overlooking the marina. She ate while waves moved beneath the moored boats.

Copper pans hung above the long counter, and afternoon light crossed the cooking classroom. Marco tied his apron while the instructor demonstrated how to fold butter into pastry dough without warming it. His first batch tore, leaking filling across the tray, but he watched more closely and began again. He chilled his hands under water, measured each turn, and tucked the pear slices into neat spirals. When the oven door opened, his tart stood crisp and golden, its layers risen like tiny pages. The instructor cut a wedge, tasted it, and nodded. “That is exactly right,” she said. Marco’s breath caught. Heat rushed through his chest and up his neck, and a grin stretched his cheeks until they ached. He laughed, clapped flour from his hands, and nearly bounced against the counter. Around him, classmates reached for samples and murmured approval. The crust shattered cleanly beneath their forks. Marco tasted one buttery bite and thought he could bake a hundred more.

Copper pans hung above the stoves in the crowded evening cooking class. Marco had spent an hour kneading pasta dough until it shone, following every instruction while his partner wandered off to sample sauces. When the instructor inspected their station, the partner stepped forward and claimed the finished ravioli as his own work. “Excellent technique,” the instructor said, handing him the class prize: a new chef’s knife. Marco opened his mouth, but the instructor waved him back to his cutting board and criticized him for not contributing. Heat surged up Marco’s neck. His jaw locked so tightly that his teeth ached, and he drove the rolling pin across a fresh lump of dough until it flattened like paper. The partner smirked and tucked the knife into his bag. Marco’s fingers curled around the counter’s edge. He imagined sweeping every gleaming pan onto the floor. Instead, he lifted the instructor’s discarded score sheet, pointed to his own signed preparation notes, and said, “Check the camera.”

Marco arrived at the cooking class and placed his coat on a hook near the door. He washed his hands, tied an apron around his waist, and stood beside a stainless-steel counter. An instructor set out bowls, knives, cutting boards, and several vegetables. Marco watched a demonstration on slicing onions, then copied the same motion at his station. He added the pieces to a pan with oil and stirred them with a wooden spoon. Other students worked at nearby counters, occasionally carrying utensils to the sink. The instructor explained how to prepare a basic sauce using tomatoes, herbs, and stock. Marco measured each ingredient, poured them into the pan, and lowered the heat. While the sauce cooked, he boiled pasta in a large pot and drained it through a colander. He combined the pasta and sauce, placed a portion on a plate, and wiped the counter. At the end, he washed his equipment, folded the apron, collected his coat, and left the room.

Marco stood at a stainless-steel counter in the crowded cooking classroom, slicing onions beside a simmering pot. The instructor demonstrated how to flambé a pan, and everyone leaned closer as blue flames curled above the sauce. When Marco tried, his hand slipped, spilling liquor across the burner and onto his apron. Fire raced up his chest. For one frozen second, he watched it climb toward his face, unable to breathe or think. Then he screamed and slapped at himself, but the flames spread along his sleeve. “Drop to the floor,” the instructor said. Marco collapsed, rolling frantically while someone smothered him with a heavy cloth. Smoke filled his nose, and his heart battered his ribs. Even after the fire was gone, he shook so hard that his teeth clicked. He stared at the blackened apron, imagining skin blistering beneath it, and recoiled when another burner hissed nearby. He backed against the wall, certain the room would ignite again.

Marco entered the cooking classroom through a red door and placed his notebook beside a row of crimson bowls. Under deep red pendant lamps, the instructor arranged tomatoes, red peppers, radishes, and ruby-colored onions on a scarlet cloth. Marco tied a burgundy apron over his shirt and selected a red-handled knife from the rack. At a vermilion counter, he diced the tomatoes while another student measured paprika into a small maroon cup. “Cut the peppers evenly,” the instructor said, pointing toward a red cutting board. Marco trimmed each pepper, then stirred the pieces into a copper pot coated with dark red enamel. Nearby, students filled brick-red dishes with beans, tomato paste, and thin slices of red onion. Marco added paprika, checked the red numerals on the wall clock, and lowered the dial on the crimson stove. When the sauce thickened to a muted garnet shade, he spooned it onto red ceramic plates. The class ended beneath the same red lamps, and Marco carried his burgundy apron home.

The evening cooking class met in a tiled kitchen above the market. Marco tied on his apron and opened the recipe booklet to mushroom ravioli, the dish his wife had taught him before she died. He had enrolled because the instructor’s advertisement promised family recipes, and he wanted to make hers without consulting the stained card she had written. As the students rolled pasta, the instructor gathered their scraps and tossed them away. Marco reached for his card too late; it slid from beneath his cutting board into the bin, then vanished under eggshells and wet coffee grounds. He dug through the refuse until the ink bled into blue clouds and her careful handwriting dissolved. “Please, let me try,” the instructor said, taking the pulp. Nothing could be saved. Marco stood over the counter, flour whitening his motionless hands. His throat closed, and tears struck the dough in dark circles. He could remember her voice saying “a pinch,” but not how much, and the missing measure felt like losing her again.

Marco entered the cooking class and placed four bowls beside a cutting board. The instructor assigned vegetable pies for six diners. Marco divided 480 grams of flour by 4, calculating 480 ÷ 4 = 120 grams for each dough portion. He measured 3 spoonfuls of oil into each of 4 bowls, so 3 × 4 = 12 spoonfuls. For the filling, he chopped 7 mushrooms into 8 slices each, recording 7 × 8 = 56 slices. He added 24 tomato pieces to the mushrooms, and 56 + 24 = 80 pieces went into the pan. Two pieces remained on the board, so 80 - 2 = 78 pieces were cooked. The class had 6 trays with 3 pies per tray, giving 6 × 3 = 18 pies. After 2 pies were set aside for demonstration, 18 - 2 = 16 remained. Marco divided those among 4 tables: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 pies per table. He washed the bowls while the pies baked.

Marco attended a cooking class in a whitewashed kitchen overlooking the harbor, where fishing boats shifted with the tide. The instructor placed bowls of mussels, seaweed, and coastal herbs beside windows flecked with seawater. Marco rinsed the mussels while small waves folded against the quay and gulls crossed above anchored ships. He sliced fennel, stirred a pale broth, and watched the surface move like a steady current along the coastline. “Add the shellfish now,” the instructor said as a ferry passed beyond the breakwater. Marco lowered each mussel into the pot, then measured salt as the incoming tide covered the harbor steps. Steam drifted toward the open window, mixing with the briny air from kelp beds and moored trawlers. When the broth thickened, he ladled it into bowls patterned with blue fish and set bread beside them. The class ate at a long table while sunlit ripples crossed the harbor and a cargo ship moved offshore.

At low tide, Hiroshi crossed the harbor road while gulls traced circles above the fishing boats. The postman approached from the pier, carrying a canvas bag marked with salt from the sea air. He handed Hiroshi a letter, then continued toward houses lined along the curving coast. Hiroshi sat on a seawall where small waves folded over black stones and opened the envelope. Inside, a shipping clerk had listed the arrival date of a cargo vessel and the number of a warehouse beside the docks. Hiroshi read the page twice as a ferry moved across the channel and left a white wake among drifting kelp. He placed the letter in his coat pocket, watching crabs travel between tide pools below the harbor wall. When the tide began covering the lowest rocks, he walked along the waterfront toward the warehouse. Behind him, the postman boarded a launch, and its engine mixed with the wash of waves against the pilings.

Yuki lived beside a harbor where seawater tapped the stone wall beneath her window. When her neighbor boarded a ferry along the coastline, Yuki agreed to look after the small brown dog for three days. Each morning, she clipped on its leash and followed a path above the tide pools, where crabs moved between shells. The dog stopped often to examine driftwood, seaweed, and ropes drying near the fishing boats. At noon, Yuki filled its bowl while gulls crossed above the masts and waves folded against the beach. “Your water is here,” she said, placing the bowl beside a window facing the sea. In the afternoon, they sat on the harbor steps as seals surfaced beyond the buoys and cargo ships passed offshore. Yuki brushed sand from the dog’s coat after each coastal walk and stored the leash near a basket of shells. On the third evening, the ferry returned across the silver tide, and the neighbor collected the dog while Yuki watched fishing lights appear along the bay.

Yuki looked after her neighbor’s dog from eight in the morning until six in the evening, a span of 10 hours because 6 + 12 - 8 = 10. The neighbor had left 12 scoops of kibble, arranged as 3 meals of 4 scoops each: 3 × 4 = 12. Yuki served the first meal at eight. At noon, she counted 8 scoops remaining, since 12 - 4 = 8, and served another 4. The dog drank from a bowl holding 900 milliliters. Yuki divided that amount into 3 equal refills, so 900 ÷ 3 = 300 milliliters per refill. During two walks, they covered 7 blocks in the morning and 5 blocks in the afternoon; 7 + 5 = 12 blocks altogether. Each block took about 3 minutes, making 12 × 3 = 36 minutes of walking. At six, 4 scoops remained, one bowl stood empty, and the dog lay beside the door until the neighbor returned.

Andrei entered the museum at 10:15 and read that the building contained 6 galleries. In the first gallery, he counted 18 ceramic bowls and 7 clay jars, calculating 18 + 7 = 25 objects. The next room displayed 32 framed maps, but 9 were temporarily covered, so he noted 32 - 9 = 23 visible maps. Along one wall, 8 shelves each held 6 mineral samples; 8 × 6 = 48 samples. A central case contained 36 coins arranged equally in 4 rows, giving 36 ÷ 4 = 9 coins per row. Andrei then climbed 24 steps to the upper floor and crossed a hall divided into 3 sections, each 12 meters long; 3 × 12 = 36 meters. A guide said, “The final gallery closes at five.” Andrei checked 14 paintings there, added them to the 23 maps, and recorded 14 + 23 = 37 works. He left through the main entrance at 12:05.

Emeka started along the mountain trail at 8:10, carrying 2 liters of water and 6 oat bars. The first marker stood 3 kilometers from the gate, and the second added 4 kilometers, so he calculated 3 + 4 = 7 kilometers. At a junction, a sign divided the remaining 12 kilometers into 3 equal sections: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 kilometers per section. He counted 5 switchbacks in each of the next 4 sections, giving 5 × 4 = 20 switchbacks. After drinking 0.25 liters twice, he worked out 2 - 0.5 = 1.5 liters left. Two hikers passed downhill while he recorded the elevation: 1,240 meters at the junction and 1,610 meters at the ridge, a gain of 1,610 - 1,240 = 370 meters. He ate 2 bars, leaving 6 - 2 = 4. At 12:10, he noted that 4 hours had passed, covering 16 kilometers, so his average was 16 ÷ 4 = 4 kilometers per hour. Then he continued toward the summit marker.

Tomas entered the public library at nine and counted 24 chairs around 6 tables, calculating 24 ÷ 6 = 4 chairs per table. He placed three books beside his notebook and recorded their page totals: 128 + 96 + 144 = 368 pages. After reading 32 pages from the first book, he noted 128 − 32 = 96 pages remaining. At a reference shelf, he found 7 volumes with 45 maps in each, so 7 × 45 = 315 maps. A librarian pushed a cart containing 36 books and divided them among 4 shelves; Tomas wrote 36 ÷ 4 = 9 books per shelf. At noon, he counted 18 visitors downstairs and 11 upstairs, making 18 + 11 = 29 visitors. Later, 8 people left, leaving 29 − 8 = 21. He copied 5 lines from each of 6 encyclopedia entries, totaling 5 × 6 = 30 lines. At four, Tomas returned his books, packed one notebook and two pencils, and walked out.

At seven fifteen, the bus crawled through rain-polished streets beneath a gray sky. Greta stood in the aisle, gripping a cold metal pole while her soaked bag bumped against her knee. When a seat finally opened, she stepped toward it, but a man shoved past and dropped into it, spreading his coat across the empty half. “I was waiting for that seat,” she said. He glanced at her swollen ankle, then turned toward the window. The driver braked hard, and pain shot up her leg as she caught herself. Heat surged into her face. Her fingers locked around the pole until the knuckles blanched, and she pictured wrenching the coat onto the filthy floor. She had paid the same fare, risen earlier, stood through three delays, yet he occupied two places as if she were invisible. At her stop, she deliberately dragged her dripping bag across his polished shoes. His protest followed her onto the pavement, where her jaw remained clenched all the way to the office.

Rain streaked the apartment windows while delivery trucks crawled along the street below. Nadia refreshed the tracking page again; the package still showed “delivered,” though the hallway, lobby, and mailroom were empty. Inside it was the medication she had ordered a week earlier, before her insurance expired. She called the courier and waited forty minutes, listening to the same clipped melody. The representative finally insisted that a driver had handed it directly to her. “That did not happen,” Nadia said. He replied that the case was closed and suggested she reorder at full price. Heat surged up her neck. Her grip tightened until the phone creaked, and she imagined the driver ticking a box without leaving the van, while the company charged her for its lie. She paced the kitchen, jaw locked, then slammed every receipt onto the table. When the call disconnected, she hurled the empty shipping envelope from an earlier order against the wall and began drafting a complaint to every regulator she could find.

The school gym held rows of science projects beneath bright ceiling lights. Sofia stood beside her homemade volcano, waiting for the judges to reach her table. As she poured vinegar into the painted crater, a sharp pop sounded behind her. A nearby display had tipped, knocking a small burner against a curtain. Orange flame crawled up the fabric. Sofia’s breath caught, and the cup slipped from her fingers. For one frozen second, she imagined the fire racing across the hanging decorations and trapping everyone inside. Heat pressed against her face as smoke curled toward the ceiling. Her heart hammered so hard that her vision pulsed. “Fire,” she managed, pointing with a shaking hand. A teacher grabbed an extinguisher while students hurried toward the exits. The flames vanished beneath white powder, but Sofia’s knees still buckled. Outside, she wrapped both arms around herself, unable to stop trembling as sirens approached the school.

Rain streaked the apartment windows while delivery vans crawled along the street below. Oskar refreshed the tracking page again: package delivered, signed by recipient. He had waited beside the door all afternoon, and no bell had rung. Downstairs, the lobby shelf stood bare. The building manager checked the camera footage and found the courier carrying Oskar’s parcel back to the van after glancing at the locked entrance. Customer service insisted the signature proved delivery and closed his claim. “That is not my signature,” Oskar said. The agent repeated the policy, then ended the call. Heat surged into his face. He gripped the phone until his knuckles blanched, imagining the courier inventing a mark and the company hiding behind it. He slammed his palm against the counter, rattling every cup, then reopened the claim form. This time he attached the footage, the blank lobby photograph, and a demand for the supervisor’s name. He would not let them erase what had happened.

The school gym held rows of poster boards, folding tables, and humming science projects beneath bright ceiling lights. Mateo stood beside his homemade volcano while judges moved down the aisle. He had mixed the chemicals carefully, but when he poured the final solution into the crater, nothing happened. A second later, the bottle beside him began to swell. Its plastic sides bulged outward, and the cap lifted with a sharp hiss. Mateo’s stomach dropped. He remembered the warning on the label: pressure could make the container burst. His hands shook so badly that he knocked over a measuring cup. Students crowded closer, blocking the nearest exit. The bottle grew rounder. Mateo pictured shards flying into their faces, and his breath came in quick, shallow pulls. “Move back,” he said, his voice cracking. He forced his stiff legs forward, grabbed a thick safety bin, and lowered it over the bottle. The cap popped against the bin with a violent bang. Mateo crouched, arms over his head, trembling long after the gym fell silent.

At noon, rain striped the windows of Bruno’s narrow apartment. The mail slot clattered, and a cream envelope slid across the floor. He recognized the law office’s seal and tore it open beside the kitchen table. The letter stated that his late father’s workshop had been awarded to a distant cousin, despite the signed will Bruno had delivered months earlier. A second page claimed his documents had arrived after the deadline. Bruno checked the receipt pinned above the sink. It showed the date clearly: six days before the deadline. Heat climbed his neck. His fingers crushed the letter until the paper split beneath his thumb. They had ignored the receipt, sold the tools he had maintained for years, and called him careless. “No,” he said. He swept a mug from the table; it struck the wall and scattered white shards across the tiles. Breathing through clenched teeth, Bruno flattened the receipt, photographed it, and reached for his coat. The office closed in twenty minutes, and this time they would look him in the eye.

Helen entered the laboratory and arranged six labeled vials beside the centrifuge. She measured 10 milliliters of buffer for each vial, calculating 6 × 10 = 60 milliliters in total. She divided the 60 milliliters among three beakers, so 60 ÷ 3 = 20 milliliters per beaker. Into each beaker she added 5 milliliters of reagent, recording 20 + 5 = 25 milliliters. Evaporation removed 4 milliliters from one beaker, leaving 25 − 4 = 21 milliliters. Helen transferred 7 milliliters from that beaker into each of three tubes, since 21 ÷ 3 = 7. She set the centrifuge to 800 rotations per minute for 6 minutes, producing 800 × 6 = 4,800 rotations. Afterward, she counted 12 colonies on one plate, 15 on another, and 13 on a third; 12 + 15 + 13 = 40 colonies. Dividing 40 by 4 sample groups gave an average of 10 colonies per group. She entered the figures in the laboratory log and stored the tubes.

The school gym held rows of folding tables beneath bright ceiling lights, each covered with posters, wires, plants, and glass jars. Wei stood beside his model volcano while judges moved down the aisle. He had built a hidden pressure chamber to produce a taller eruption, but as he reached for the switch, he noticed the plastic bottle swelling beneath the painted mountain. A sharp crack split the cardboard base. The volcano tilted toward a crowded table where students leaned over open chemical samples. Wei’s mouth went dry. His pulse hammered against his throat, and his fingers stiffened above the switch. The bottle bulged again, stretching white at the seams. It could burst, spraying vinegar and dye into the electrical strip below. “Move back,” he whispered. No one heard. His knees shook as he lunged forward, yanked the plug, and dragged the volcano onto the floor. The bottle ruptured with a heavy pop. Red foam soaked his shoes, and Wei stood gasping, unable to unclench his hands.

Rain striped the apartment windows when the mail dropped through Hiroshi’s brass slot. He sorted the envelopes beside the cold stove and found one bearing the seal of the housing office. Three months earlier, he had submitted every receipt proving that the landlord had charged illegal fees. The letter stated that his complaint was dismissed because no receipts had been provided. Hiroshi read the sentence twice. Heat climbed his neck, and his fingers creased the paper until the seal split. Attached was a photocopy of his own evidence, stamped RECEIVED. Someone had handled it, copied it, and then claimed it did not exist. “So that is their answer,” he said. He drove his fist against the table, rattling the cups, then swept the unpaid bills onto the floor. His jaw ached from clenching. They expected him to surrender because their desk stood between him and justice. He flattened the letter, circled the contradiction in red, and reached for a fresh envelope.

Late sunlight stretched across the muddy municipal pitch as two amateur teams lined up for kickoff. Beatriz played on the right wing, chasing loose balls and crossing toward the crowded goalmouth. Midway through the second half, she slipped past a defender and struck low into the corner. The referee pointed to the center, then reversed the decision after the opposing captain protested, claiming Beatriz had handled the ball. She stared at the official. Her arms had been pinned against her ribs. “That never touched my hand,” she said. The referee waved her away and booked her for dissent. Heat surged up her neck. Her jaw locked so hard her teeth ached, and every smug glance from the defenders scraped at her. On the next attack, one of them hauled her down by the shirt. The whistle stayed silent. Beatriz slapped the mud with both palms, sprang up, and drove after the ball, thinking she would tear through every unfair obstacle they put before her.

At seven fifteen, the bus hissed beside the rain-dark curb while office towers blurred behind low clouds. Ingrid climbed aboard, tapped her pass, and moved toward the only empty seat. Before she reached it, a man dropped his briefcase across the cushion and stared through the window. “I was sitting there,” he said. She pointed to the priority sign above him and then to the brace strapped around her knee. The driver glanced back but waved her down the aisle, though two other passengers had been allowed to keep bags on seats. At the next turn, Ingrid’s knee buckled, and her coffee splashed across her coat. Heat surged up her neck. Her jaw locked until her teeth hurt. The man smirked and pulled his briefcase closer, guarding the seat as if she were a thief. Ingrid gripped the overhead rail, imagining the case hurled into the aisle. Instead, she photographed the bus number, the blocked seat, and the driver’s badge. By her stop, her hands shook, but the complaint was already sent.

The overnight train crossed the plains beneath a sky streaked with winter clouds. Ana had been aboard for twelve hours when the conductor stopped beside her berth and demanded another ticket. She produced the stamped paper she had shown twice already, but he glanced at it and declared it invalid. “Pay again or leave at the next station,” he said. Across the aisle, passengers with identical tickets remained unchallenged. Ana pointed this out, yet he turned away and blocked the corridor with his cart. Heat surged up her neck. Her fingers crushed the ticket until its edges cut her palm. She pictured the hours she had worked to afford the journey, then saw the conductor smirking as he collected her money. Each wheel strike hammered the insult deeper. At the next stop, she marched past him, found the station supervisor, and slapped the crumpled ticket and receipt onto the desk. She would not move until every coin was returned and his conduct recorded.

Ilse’s flight landed at 10:20, and her connection departed at 13:50, so she calculated 13:50 − 10:20 = 3 hours 30 minutes. The departure board listed 18 gates in one concourse and 12 in another; 18 + 12 = 30 gates. She walked past 6 seating zones, each containing 8 rows, and recorded 6 × 8 = 48 rows. At a café, 24 passengers occupied 6 tables, giving 24 ÷ 6 = 4 passengers per table. Ilse filled her bottle, then counted 17 aircraft through the left windows and 9 through the right ones; 17 + 9 = 26 aircraft. At 11:35, she subtracted the time already used: 75 minutes had passed, leaving 210 − 75 = 135 minutes. She divided that interval into three equal parts, 135 ÷ 3 = 45 minutes each: walking, reading, and sitting near Gate 22. Boarding began at 13:20, exactly 30 minutes before departure.

The overnight train crossed the northern plains beneath a sky crowded with winter stars. Ana had been aboard for fourteen hours, watching stations pass like brief islands of light, when the carriage suddenly lurched and stopped inside a mountain tunnel. The lamps flickered out. Somewhere ahead, metal shrieked against metal, followed by three heavy blows beneath the floor. Passengers stirred, raising phone screens, but there was no signal and no announcement. Then smoke slipped through the ventilation grille. Ana’s hands began shaking so violently that she dropped her water bottle. Her pulse hammered in her throat. She pictured flames racing through the sealed carriages and found herself counting the narrow windows, knowing none would open. A child started coughing. “Move toward the rear,” someone said. Ana stumbled into the aisle as another blow jolted the train. The darkness seemed to tighten around her. When an emergency lamp finally glowed and the rear door opened, she ran with the others, unable to draw a full breath until cold tunnel air struck her face.

Rain striped the windows of Jonas’s empty house while the estate agent arranged contracts across the kitchen counter. After months of viewings, Jonas had accepted an offer well below his asking price because the buyer promised a quick sale. Now, minutes before signing, the buyer’s solicitor announced another reduction, citing a cracked garden tile and “general uncertainty.” Jonas stared at the new figure. The tile had appeared in every survey, and the buyer had already demanded money off for it. “That was included in the agreed price,” he said. The solicitor shrugged and began packing the papers, explaining that the buyer would walk away unless Jonas conceded. Heat surged up Jonas’s neck. His jaw locked so tightly that his teeth hurt. They had waited until his removal van was booked, his mortgage approved, and his furniture gone. He pictured them counting on his helplessness. His fist struck the counter, making the keys jump. “Then let them walk.” He tore the amended page in half and held the door open until the solicitor left.

At nine on Tuesday evening, rain threaded down the kitchen window while Pavel sorted unopened bills beneath the yellow lamp. His phone rang, and his younger brother’s number flashed across the screen. Pavel answered, expecting another request for money. Instead, his brother said their mother’s house had been sold that afternoon. “You signed away your share last year.” Pavel stood so quickly that the chair struck the wall. He remembered the hospital corridor, the stack of forms, and his brother pointing to a page described as permission to manage repairs. No one had mentioned surrendering ownership. His brother added that the proceeds were already in a private account and ended the call. Heat surged up Pavel’s neck. He dialed back, but every attempt went straight to voicemail. His jaw locked until his teeth hurt. He swept the bills from the table, then slammed his palm down hard enough to rattle the lamp. All those weekends fixing the roof, all those promises, converted into a trick and a blocked number. He grabbed his coat and the folder of copied forms.

Priya counted twelve envelopes in the apartment mailbox, and one carried her name in blue ink. She took it upstairs, placed it beside three circulars, and calculated that 12 minus 3 equaled 9 remaining pieces for the other tenants. The postmark was dated October 2, and the calendar showed October 8: six days had passed because 8 minus 2 equaled 6. After opening the flap, she found two sheets, each with 24 words, so 2 times 24 equaled 48 words. The sender had listed 36 cuttings from a shared garden, divided among 4 recipients; 36 divided by 4 equaled 9 cuttings each. A paragraph recorded 17 tomato plants and 15 bean plants, giving 17 plus 15 equaled 32 plants. Priya checked the enclosed table: five rows held 7 entries apiece, and 5 times 7 equaled 35 entries. She marked one discrepancy, since 35 minus 32 equaled 3. At the desk, she wrote a reply of 60 words across 3 equal sections, calculating 60 divided by 3 equaled 20 words per section.

The overnight train carried Carlos north through mountain tunnels and snow-covered valleys. After fourteen hours, most passengers slept beneath dim lamps, while he watched his reflection tremble in the window. Deep inside a tunnel, the brakes shrieked and the carriage slammed sideways, flinging luggage from the racks. A burnt smell seeped through the vents. Then the lights failed. Somewhere ahead, metal boomed, followed by a thin hiss and footsteps pounding along the roof. Carlos gripped his seat as his pulse hammered against his throat. His mouth dried; each breath came shallow and sharp. When smoke curled under the connecting door, he pictured flames racing through the sealed cars and the mountain collapsing above them. He lunged for the emergency handle, but it would not move. Passengers woke, coughing and shoving toward the exits. The hiss grew louder. Carlos pressed his back to the cold glass, knees shaking, certain the next sound would be the tunnel giving way.

Rain striped the apartment windows while the brass mail slot clicked at noon. Beatriz opened the envelope and unfolded a letter from the university. It said her scholarship had been revoked because she had failed to submit her income form, and that the appeal deadline had expired the previous day. Beneath the notice, a clerk’s stamp showed the form had been received three weeks earlier. She read both dates again. Heat climbed her throat, and her fingers crushed the paper until its edge cut her palm. The award had been the only way she could enroll; now their mistake had locked the door and blamed her for standing outside. She called the number at the bottom. A recorded voice told her no appeals could be accepted. “You received it,” she said through clenched teeth. When the message repeated, she slammed the receiver down, swept the bills from the table, and drove her fist into the wall. Plaster dust fell across the letter as she reached for the phone again.

Rain striped the studio windows while Leila sat at the upright piano. Halfway through the lesson, her teacher knocked the metronome from its shelf while reaching for a pencil. Its wooden case split against the floor. Before Leila could speak, the teacher called her careless and declared that the repair cost would be added to her next lesson. “I never touched it,” Leila said. The teacher waved her objection aside and ordered her to begin the sonata again. Heat rushed up Leila’s neck. Her fingers struck the opening chord so hard that the keys clacked beneath it. She played faster than the markings allowed, each note sharp and punishing. When the teacher tapped the page to stop her, Leila kept going, jaw locked, pulse hammering in her wrists. She thought of the falling metronome, the lie, the effortless dismissal. At the final measure, she slammed both palms onto the keyboard, stood, and placed the lesson fee back in her own pocket.

Tuesday sunlight fell across the glass conference-room table on the twelfth floor. Amara sat opposite three interviewers, her portfolio open beside a printed copy of the job description. After an hour of technical questions, the manager slid her design proposal back and said, “This is exactly the direction we need.” Yet when Amara asked about the salary, another interviewer folded his hands and offered fifteen thousand less than the advertised minimum. He explained that she lacked leadership experience, though they had spent twenty minutes praising the team she had led. Heat surged up her neck. Her molars pressed together until her jaw throbbed. On the table lay their notes, including a highlighted line: managed twelve staff. The manager then asked whether she could prove herself for six months at the lower rate. Amara closed her portfolio with deliberate care. They wanted her work, her plans, and her authority, but not to pay for any of it. “Then you cannot afford me,” she said, rising and leaving without offering her hand.

Martha waited beside her sedan in a repair shop at the edge of town. A mechanic replaced a cracked brake hose and told her the car was ready. She paid, thanked him, and drove toward the highway. At the first intersection, the brake pedal sank to the floor. The sedan rolled through a red light as a truck thundered across her path. Martha yanked the wheel, missing its trailer by inches, and bounced onto the shoulder. Her hands locked around the steering wheel. Her pulse hammered in her throat, and cold sweat spread beneath her coat. The car kept rolling downhill toward a crowded crosswalk. She pumped the useless pedal and dragged the parking brake upward. “Stop, please stop,” she whispered. Metal shrieked. The sedan spun, struck the curb, and stalled beside a lamppost. Martha sat rigid while pedestrians scattered. Even after the engine went silent, her knees shook, and every passing vehicle made her flinch.

Saturday sunlight striped the municipal football pitch as two amateur teams assembled beside the halfway line. Priya tightened her borrowed boots and took her place in defence. The match began briskly, with uneven passes, shouted instructions, and spectators leaning over the rail. Midway through the second half, an opposing striker broke clear. Priya sprinted across and hooked the ball away, but the striker stumbled over her leg and struck the ground without moving. A teammate knelt beside the player, then waved urgently toward the sideline. “Call an ambulance,” someone said. Priya stood frozen. Her pulse hammered against her throat, and each breath stopped halfway into her lungs. She stared at the player’s still hands and imagined bones broken, a life ended, police arriving, everyone pointing at her. The whistle slipped from the referee’s fingers. Priya’s knees shook so violently that she crouched, pressing both palms into the grass. At last, the striker coughed and rolled onto one elbow, but Priya still could not unclench her jaw.

Kofi stood alone in the basement laboratory beside a sealed reaction chamber. He checked the pressure gauge, adjusted the coolant valve, and injected the final reagent through a narrow port. For several seconds, the mixture remained clear. Then it darkened, boiling without heat, and the gauge needle snapped past the red limit. An alarm began pulsing overhead. Kofi reached for the emergency cutoff, but the switch sparked beneath his glove. The chamber shuddered, and a thin crack appeared across its viewing window. His breath caught. Sweat chilled his neck as he backed toward the exit, unable to look away from the widening line. If the glass failed, the toxic vapor would fill the room before the ventilation system engaged. He pulled the door handle. It did not move. “Open,” he whispered. Another crack branched across the window.
